# Languages

Field's small languages, from the host side. A box can be *written* in one of them — a per-box property picks the language and a `BoxExecution` runs it, which is how `datalog`, `forth`, `nano`, `morpho`, `clojure`, `python`, FieldML and the two `remotejs` runtimes work — or a program can be *embedded*, a triple-quoted Kotlin string whose first line names the language and whose contents are compiled on the JVM, which is how RectSL and StackSL work. What is documented below is the Kotlin that either shape hands you: the compiler you give a program to, the result and the diagnostics it gives back, and the bridge a running program calls host values through. The notation itself is on the cheatsheets, and that is where the pictures are. Read `Datalog.kt` first — it is the smallest complete example of the shape all of these have, a value you add source to, query, and then ask `why` of — then `DatalogEngine.kt` for what the implementation underneath actually costs, `StackSL.kt` for the compile-and-diagnose surface both embedded languages share, `ForthInterpreter.kt` and `NanoVM.kt` for the two implementations you can read end to end in a sitting, and `HostBridge.kt` for FieldML's reflective JVM bridge — the file to read before wiring any language to Kotlin values. `dev_docs/` carries the map of what a new language has to touch on the way in, in `small_language_anatomy.md`, which is also the guarded list of which languages exist. The prose, with pictures: [Language extensions](../language_extensions.md) for the route decision, then [Datalog](../datalog.md), [RectSL](../rectsl_cheatsheet.md), [StackSL](../stacksl_cheatsheet.md), [FieldML](../fieldml_cheatsheet.md), [MorphoHDL](../morpho_examples.md), [Nano](../nano_examples.md), [Forth](../forth_examples.md) and [Python](../python.md).

## Datalog.kt { #datalog-kt }

The facade over parser and engine: a [`Datalog`](languages.md#datalog-kt-datalog) holds a program, answers queries as [`DlRows`](languages.md#datalog-kt-dlrows), and
reconstructs the proof of a derived fact.

Nothing here parses or evaluates. [`DatalogParser`](languages.md#datalogparser-kt-datalogparser) turns text into the [`DlUnit`](languages.md#datalogast-kt-dlunit) this file merges
and [`DatalogEngine`](languages.md#datalogengine-kt-datalogengine) computes the model; what is left is the part a caller touches — holding the
program, noticing when the cached model has gone stale, and sorting rows so that a query prints
the same way twice, which set semantics on their own do not promise.

The exception is the top-down proof search behind `why`, which is here rather than in the engine
because it reads a finished model instead of building one. It walks rules backwards from a
derived fact, bounded by the round numbers the fixpoint recorded, and picks premises in the same
order the planner would. The opposite question, why a goal has no answers at all, is
`DatalogWhyNot.kt`.

`import afield.data.query.datalog.*` is in every Kotlin box's preamble, so `Datalog()` and the `Dl` types
are in scope with nothing to import.

## DatalogAst.kt { #datalogast-kt }

The abstract syntax of Field's Datalog — see [`Datalog`](languages.md#datalog-kt-datalog) for the facade, [`DatalogParser`](languages.md#datalogparser-kt-datalogparser) for the
concrete syntax and [`DatalogEngine`](languages.md#datalogengine-kt-datalogengine) for what evaluates this.

Everything here is a value type with structural equality, because the engine leans on that in two
places: rules are de-duplicated when the same text is executed twice (a live box re-runs its whole
program on every keystroke-triggered execute), and derived rows are stored in hash sets.

Names are `Dl`-prefixed. Boxes get `import afield.data.query.datalog.*` for free (see
`afield.document.graph.intro`), on top of the standard document, geometry and math imports, so an unprefixed `Var`, `Atom` or
`Rule` in this package would be a name collision waiting to happen in user code.

### DlConst { #datalogast-kt-dlconst }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DlConst</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DlTerm</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/query/datalog/DatalogAst/#L34)

## DatalogBoxes.kt { #datalogboxes-kt }

The Field bridge: the live box graph as Datalog base relations.

This is the reason for having a Datalog in here rather than shelling out to one. A Field document
*is* a labelled graph — boxes, parent/child edges, nesting, and a property bag per box — and the
questions you actually ask of it while working ("which boxes does nothing run into?", "which two
boxes both bind the same property?", "what is downstream of this one?") are recursive joins,
which is precisely what `afield.data.query.graph`'s path language cannot express and this can.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val d = Datalog()
d.addBoxGraph(thisBox)
d.add("""
    reaches(A, B) :- child(A, B).
    reaches(A, C) :- reaches(A, B), child(B, C).
    orphan(X) :- box(X), !child(_, X).
""")
println(d.query("orphan(X), name(X, N)").table())
```

## DatalogEditorExtension.kt { #datalogeditorextension-kt }

Serves `datalog.js`, the browser-side Datalog editor support, to the page and to the test that
checks it.

The JavaScript is the implementation and this file is a reader for it. `datalog.js` lives in
`src/commonMain/resources`, reaches the browser as the AMD module `bithero/datalog` (one of the
modules `bootstrapMonaco.js` requires by name while the editor starts), and is read back verbatim
here, so the smoke test `datalog.editor-extension.workout` runs the same bytes the editor does. A
browser-side language that can only be tested in a browser does not stay correct.

Once installed, the extension brings syntax highlighting, lexical diagnostics, a context badge
and completions to `#datalog` regions embedded in Kotlin triple-quoted strings, and to whole
`.datalog` documents. Colouring is decoration-based rather than a Monarch grammar, so one tokenizer covers
both contexts and there is no grammar here that can fail to compile and take Monaco's startup down
with it. The same workout also compares the editor's vocabulary against `DatalogParser`'s, since
the editor is JavaScript in a browser and the parser is Kotlin on a server, and the two lists can
only be kept in step at build time.

`datalog.js` installs itself either way it is loaded: as an AMD module when a Monaco loader
is present, and immediately when it is evaluated bare, which is the path `html()` uses.

## DatalogEngine.kt { #datalogengine-kt }

Storage and evaluation: indexed relations, a safety-directed body planner, stratification, and a
semi-naive fixpoint.

Three invariants hold the thing together, and each one buys a feature:

 - **Rows are planned, not interpreted.** Each rule is compiled once into a list of `DlStep`s over
   integer variable slots, and the planner decides statically whether each argument position binds
   or filters. Nothing consults a "is this variable bound yet" map at join time.
 - **Facts derived in a round are not visible until the round ends.** New rows go to a pending
   buffer and are merged at the end of the iteration, so every fact's [`DlRelation.roundOf`](languages.md#datalogengine-kt--dlrelation--roundof) is
   strictly greater than the rounds of the facts that derived it. That is what makes
   [`Datalog.why`](languages.md#datalog-kt--datalog--why) terminate without an occurs-check hack: a proof may only descend to
   strictly earlier rounds. The counter is *global*, not per-stratum, so the same ordering holds
   across a stratum boundary and a proof may descend through negation and aggregation too.
 - **Negation and aggregation are stratified.** Both are "negative" edges in the dependency graph;
   a negative edge inside a strongly-connected component is rejected up front with the cycle
   spelled out, rather than producing an answer that depends on evaluation order.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/data/query/datalog/DatalogEngine.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/data/query/datalog/DatalogEngine/)

## DatalogInterface.kt { #dataloginterface-kt }

Datalog as a box language: the [`DatalogExecution`](languages.md#dataloginterface-kt-datalogexecution) that runs fragments inside a box, and the
registration that puts Datalog in the Main Language menu.

[`DatalogExecution`](languages.md#dataloginterface-kt-datalogexecution) is the `BoxExecution`. It merges a fragment into the box's accumulated
program, prints whatever that fragment asked for, and completes on the relations the box has
actually defined as well as on the builtin functions, the aggregate operators and the box-graph
names. `installDatalog` registers the runtime and the persistent `isDatalogRoot` flag, and
`datalogTopologyNeedsUpdating` attaches and detaches executions as boxes are marked and unmarked.

The `#directives` are the Field-specific part, and the reason this is more than a thin adapter:
`#boxes` loads the live document into the base relations of [`dlBoxRelationSchema`](languages.md#datalogboxes-kt--dlboxrelationschema), `#why` and
`#whynot` reach the two provenance layers, and `#program` prints back what the box has
accumulated. `directiveHelp` is the one list that `#help` prints and completion offers, so a
directive added to it appears in both.

## DatalogLineNotes.kt { #dataloglinenotes-kt }

Line notes for a Datalog box ([`LineNotes`](workspace.md#linenotes-kt-linenotes)): what a line's statement means in the model the box's
runs have built.

A Datalog box accumulates: every run merges its facts and rules into one program, and the saturated
model of that program is the state the box is in. So a note needs no record of the last run — it
asks the model, and asking is pure. A rule's note is the facts it derives there (its body, evaluated
over the model, projected onto its head), a query's its answers, a fact's whether it is in the model
and which rules read its relation. A statement the model does not hold — text written or changed
since the line last ran — says so, rather than answering for text the model has never seen.
Directives are never run for a note: `#reset` and `#boxes` change the model.

## DatalogObjects.kt { #datalogobjects-kt }

Any live object graph as Datalog base relations, by way of `afield.data.query.graph`.

The two layers answer different halves of the same question. `graphPaths` addresses slots by
pattern and hands back live lenses, but a glob cannot follow an edge and then follow it again, and
it has nothing to say about two addresses that turn out to be the same object. Datalog has
recursion, negation and aggregation and no idea what an object is. Joining them costs one walk:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val d = Datalog()
d.addObjectGraph(rig)
d.add(dlObjectGraphRules)
d.query("alias(A, B)")                                  // two names for one object
d.query("reaches(\"carrier\", P), writable(P)")         // settable, anywhere below carrier
```

Identity is what makes it worth the trip. [`dlObjectGraphSchema`](languages.md#datalogobjects-kt--dlobjectgraphschema)'s `at(Path, ObjectId)` gives every
non-scalar value a number, so aliasing needs no special relation — it is a join of `at` with
itself. The walk already visits a shared node under every alias (its cycle detection is
path-scoped, not visit-once), so the facts are there to be joined.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/data/query/datalog/DatalogObjects.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/data/query/datalog/DatalogObjects/)

## DatalogParser.kt { #datalogparser-kt }

Source text to abstract syntax: the lexer and recursive-descent parser every Datalog program in
Field goes through, and the two word lists that decide what the notation reserves.

There is no error recovery. The first thing the parser cannot read raises a [`DlException`](languages.md#datalogast-kt-dlexception)
carrying the line and column it stopped at, and the box language turns those into an error marker
on the offending line, so a program is either whole or it is a single message.

Two of the tables outlive the parse. `DatalogParser.functions` and `DatalogParser.aggregateOps`
are what the box language offers in its completion popup, and the browser-side highlighter keeps
its own copy of both; `afield.examples.datalog.DatalogEditorExtensionWorkout` runs the shipped
JavaScript against these sets and fails when the two have drifted apart.

## DatalogSmokeTest.kt { #datalogsmoketest-kt }

Smoke test for the Datalog deductive-database language in `afield.data.query.datalog`.

Like the `afield.data.query.graph` smoke this is a plain `jvm-main` entrypoint, which works
because the engine touches no `Runloop`, starts no threads and opens no devices, so the JVM exits
naturally (see the `smoke-tests-natural-exit` convention). The live box-graph bridge
(`DatalogBoxes.kt`) and the box language live outside what this file imports.

The central case is `testSemiNaiveAgreesWithBfs`: the incremental fixpoint must produce exactly
the transitive closure an independent breadth-first search produces, over a random graph with
cycles. The other cases pin individual semantics: recursion, negation and stratification,
arithmetic, aggregates, safety errors and the query API.

## DatalogWhyNot.kt { #datalogwhynot-kt }

The why-not layer: `Datalog.whyNot` walks a failing conjunction literal by literal and names the
one that took the answer count to zero.

`Datalog.why` accounts for a fact that is present. This accounts for a query that is empty, which
is the commoner question and the one a saturated model cannot be asked directly. [`DlWhyNot`](languages.md#datalogwhynot-kt-dlwhynot) is
the result, [`DlNarrowing`](languages.md#datalogwhynot-kt-dlnarrowing) one step of the walk, and `#whynot <goal>` in a Datalog box is the way
in.

Everything here is written against the public [`Datalog`](languages.md#datalog-kt-datalog) surface, which is why it is a file of its
own rather than more of the fixpoint's. The counts it reports are the engine's rather than a
second implementation's: each prefix of the conjunction is synthesised into a rule and put
through [`DatalogEngine`](languages.md#datalogengine-kt-datalogengine), at a cost of one solve per literal.

## ClojureInterface.kt { #clojureinterface-kt }

Clojure as a Field main language: a box whose source is Clojure, evaluated by the real Clojure
runtime on this JVM.

Nothing here implements a Lisp. `clojure.jar` is on the classpath and this file is the adapter
between Field's box-execution contract and `clojure.java.api.Clojure` — which is why the whole
language is one file while `afield.data.query.datalog` and `afield.lang.rectsl`, whose compilers Field owns, are
packages.

Read it in four layers:

 - [`ClojureHost`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojurehost) is the interpreter, and the only part with no Field in it. It reads one top-level
   form at a time and evaluates it, which is `load-string`'s own loop written out so that the
   *line* each form started on is available while that form runs: that line is what lets printed
   output land beside the form that printed it, the way it does in every other kind of Field box.
   It returns the value of the last form, and `executeIfFn` will invoke that value when it is an
   `IFn` — a host convenience, off on the box path ([`ClojureExecution`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureexecution) passes `false`), so a box
   whose last form evaluates to a function prints the function rather than calling it.
   `compileOnly` is the same read loop with evaluation withheld, which is where the editor's
   syntax errors come from, carrying line and column.
 - [`ClojureInterface`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureinterface) is the host facade: the box currently running, and the handful of Field
   verbs that are awkward to reach by raw interop because they are Kotlin extension functions
   with default arguments. `field/core.clj` (in `src/jvmMain/resources`) is the Clojure side of
   it, `require`d and `refer`red into every box namespace, so a box can say `(lines ls :fit true)`
   rather than naming `SomeSkikoKt`.
 - [`ClojureExecution`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureexecution) is the `BoxExecution`, so it is the half that knows about boxes: output
   proxying, `is-running`, per-fragment generation counting, and `complete`, whose candidates
   come from Compliment if that namespace loads. Without it on the classpath `complete` returns
   an empty list rather than throwing, so a box runs and completes nothing.
 - [`installClojure`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt--installclojure) and [`clojureTopologyNeedsUpdating`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt--clojuretopologyneedsupdating) are the registration, and they are
   identical in shape to every other main language: one `registerMainLanguageRuntime` call, one
   `TopologyWatcher` that swaps a child box's execution when the graph changes.

One namespace, not one per box: every Clojure box in every open document evaluates in `live.user`
(Clojure namespaces are per-JVM, and [`ClojureExecution`](languages.md#clojureinterface-kt-clojureexecution) asks for that one name), so two Clojure
boxes are two cells of one notebook. `public/docs/clojure.md` is the page that says so to a
reader; `dev_docs/small_language_anatomy.md` is the map of the integration points.

## FieldMLCompiler.kt { #fieldmlcompiler-kt }

FieldML's front end behind one call: source text in, and whatever its four stages managed to
produce out.

[`FieldMLCompiler`](languages.md#fieldmlcompiler-kt-fieldmlcompiler) runs the lexer, the parser, the inferencer and the lowerer in turn, stopping at
the first one to report an error. What the earlier stages produced is kept either way, so a
program that does not compile still carries a token list, usually a surface tree, and sometimes a
typed tree. [`FieldMLCompletionEngine`](languages.md#fieldmlcompletionengine-kt-fieldmlcompletionengine) is built on that: it compiles a half-written line and reads
the names in scope off the typed tree, or the constructor declarations off the surface tree when
inference has given up.

Each stage lives in its own package under `afield.lang.fieldml`, and this file is where the order they go
in is written down.

## FieldMLCompletionEngine.kt { #fieldmlcompletionengine-kt }

Completion and hover for a FieldML box: what the editor offers under the caret, and what the
card over a symbol says.

The difficulty is that the text is half-written, so the compiler will usually refuse it. Both
entry points compile the box anyway and read the typed tree if one came back. When none did,
they fall back to compiling the top-level statements above the caret and keeping the longest
run of them that does compile, skipping the broken ones rather than stopping at the first,
because the broken one is normally the line being typed. Below that is a regex over `let`, `fun`
and lambda parameters, which finds the names in scope without their types.

Which *kind* of thing can go under the caret is decided before any candidate is gathered, and
two of those contexts answer with nothing rather than falling through: inside the string
literal of a `host…` intrinsic, and after a record field's dot, a member is the only thing that
can legally follow, so an empty list is the right answer when no member matches. Falling
through to the general list there is how `img.wi` came to offer the `with` keyword.

Everywhere else the list is five sources merged and deduplicated — snippets, keywords, the
prelude, the bindings in scope, and the constructors this box declared — sorted by a rank that
puts the closest thing first: a typed local binding at 0, a snippet at 10, a constructor at 16,
the graphics prelude at 18, the rest of the prelude at 24, the `host…` names at 34, and a
keyword last at 40. A `|>` to the left of the caret switches the prelude to a second table for
any name whose final argument accepts what the pipe is carrying, which is what floats `moveTo`,
`map` and the rest of `pipePreferred` to the top of a pipeline.

`hostTap`'s completions are the one place this reads something other than the box: it lists and
describes Kotlin extension functions out of Field's own source, through `KotlinSourceIndex`.

## FieldMLInterface.kt { #fieldmlinterface-kt }

FieldML as a box language: set a box's Main Language to FieldML and its children hold FieldML
programs instead of Kotlin.

[`FieldMLExecution`](languages.md#fieldmlinterface-kt-fieldmlexecution) is the `BoxExecution` behind that, one per box. It hands the text to
[`FieldMLCompiler`](languages.md#fieldmlcompiler-kt-fieldmlcompiler), evaluates the core tree that came back against [`FieldMLRuntimePrelude`](languages.md#fieldmlruntimeprelude-kt-fieldmlruntimeprelude), and
writes the value and its inferred type into the box as one inline `value : type` line. A program
that printed something of its own gets no inline line, which is what the file's `TrackingOutput`
is watching for. `display` does not count as printing, so a box that draws still says what it
evaluated to.

Nothing survives between runs. Each run compiles its text from scratch and evaluates it against
a freshly built prelude, so a FieldML box is the script model rather than the accumulating one a
Datalog box uses. State that has to outlive a run goes in a box property, which is what the
prelude's `prop` and `once` are for.

Executing and launching differ in one thing, and it is the thing that makes animation work. Both
compile and evaluate. Launch also hands the result to `ReturnValueRegistry`, the same machinery a
Kotlin box's return value goes through, so the `Sequence` that `animate` returns is advanced once
per run loop frame for as long as the box is running, while a plain number is simply the answer.
The run generation counted around that is how a second launch supersedes the first rather than
running beside it.

Which boxes are FieldML is decided by `fieldMLTopologyNeedsUpdating`, and the answer is about
parents: a box runs FieldML because a *parent* carries `isFieldMLRoot` or names `fieldml` as its
main language, not because it carries the mark itself.

## FieldMLMacroLayer.kt { #fieldmlmacrolayer-kt }

Reaching Field's Kotlin source macros from FieldML: a table of every macro `MacroRegistry`
registers, with the route to each one, and the expansion that follows the route.

FieldML is an interpreter, with no Kotlin compile anywhere in its path, so a macro whose output
is generated Kotlin has nothing to hand that output to. Each macro therefore falls into one of
three cases: it rewrites its call site to an ordinary `Box` extension function, which can be
expanded for its side effects and then called reflectively; or it generates a declaration whose
effect FieldML's own prelude implements natively; or it needs a Kotlin compiler, and only its
generated text is available. `dev_docs/FIELDML_HOST_BRIDGE.md` calls this mechanism A.

The table is a reading of the macro layer, so it can be wrong. A test holds it to the live
contents of `MacroRegistry` in both directions.

## FieldMLRuntimePrelude.kt { #fieldmlruntimeprelude-kt }

The value behind every prelude name: what a FieldML program can call before it declares
anything.

`FieldMLTypePrelude` gives the same list of names their types; this file implements them, and
the two are matched by hand rather than derived from one another. [`values`](languages.md#fieldmlruntimeprelude-kt--fieldmlruntimeprelude--values) builds the map afresh
for each run, which is how `print`, `thisBox` and the `prop` family come to mean *this* box's
output and *this* box rather than a global.

Two distinctions in here decide what a FieldML program can get away with:

- **Checking versus coercing.** A native function unpacks its arguments through the `as…`
  helpers, which refuse a value of the wrong kind and name what they found instead, so
  anything that reached the runtime as an unchecked `Host` stops here with a sentence rather
  than a default. The `hostAs…` family is why there are two sets of helpers rather than one:
  those convert, since saying what a value that arrived through an erased JVM signature
  really is is the whole of their job.
- **Reading versus writing a box property.** `prop` and `propOr` search up the box graph, so a
  value an ancestor wrote is visible; `once` reads only its own box's slot; and `setProp`
  always writes locally, shadowing an ancestor rather than changing it. Writing also narrows an
  integer or a float to the JVM width already in the slot, which is what keeps a `prop<Int>`
  shared with a Kotlin box from throwing `ClassCastException` on the Kotlin side.

`hostTap` is the one name that goes looking in Field's own source rather than at a class: it
resolves a Kotlin extension function by name through `KotlinSourceIndex` when an index is
loaded, and by walking `src/jvmMain/kotlin` and `src/personal/kotlin` when none is.

## FieldMLSourceIndex.kt { #fieldmlsourceindex-kt }

FieldML's read of the shared Kotlin source index, and the staleness check that decides whether to
trust it.

[`KotlinSourceIndex`](workspace.md#kotlinsourceindex-kt-kotlinsourceindex) holds a database of every declaration in the checkout, which FieldML wants for
three lookups: the host functions a FieldML program may call ([`FieldMLRuntimePrelude`](languages.md#fieldmlruntimeprelude-kt-fieldmlruntimeprelude)), and the
Kotlin class names and function names its completion offers ([`FieldMLCompletionEngine`](languages.md#fieldmlcompletionengine-kt-fieldmlcompletionengine)). That
database is a snapshot, so it is handed back only when every path it records still resolves to a
file. When one does not, the host-function and function-name lookups walk `src/` themselves
instead, and the class-name lookup goes quiet rather than offering stale names.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/fieldml/FieldMLSourceIndex.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/fieldml/FieldMLSourceIndex/)

## Expr.kt { #expr-kt }

FieldML's surface syntax tree: one node per piece of written syntax, each carrying the source
range it was parsed from.

[`Parser`](languages.md#parser-kt-parser) produces this tree and [`Inferencer`](languages.md#inferencer-kt-inferencer) reads it. Nothing in it has a type yet. Every node
here has a counterpart in `afield.lang.fieldml.type` that carries an inferred type, and that typed tree is
lowered again into the `afield.lang.fieldml.core` form the evaluator runs.

The tree is narrower than the syntax in two places. [`ECall`](languages.md#expr-kt-ecall) takes a single argument, so
application is already curried when it is parsed: `add 20 22` is `ECall(ECall(add, 20), 22)`. The
pipe operator builds that same node with its left operand as the argument, so `10 |> add 5` and
`add 5 10` differ only in the ranges they record. And a constructor's argument types are bare
names: [`TypeRef`](languages.md#expr-kt-typeref) has one case, [`TypeRefName`](languages.md#expr-kt-typerefname), so a run of names in `type Tree a = Node Tree Tree`
reads as a run of separate arguments. Inference resolves each name to a built-in type, to the type
being declared, to one of that type's own parameters, or to a data type with no arguments.

It is wider than the syntax in one place: [`ELet`](languages.md#expr-kt-elet) and [`ELambda`](languages.md#expr-kt-elambda) keep the parameter list as it was
written, so `let add a b = ...` is one node with two parameters. Folding those into nested arrow
types is inference's job, and turning them into nested one-parameter lambdas is the lowering's.

[`ELet`](languages.md#expr-kt-elet) and [`ETypeDecl`](languages.md#expr-kt-etypedecl) both carry a `body`, and for a top-level binding that body is the whole
rest of the program: a box's bindings stack up by nesting inside each other. A `let` with nothing
after it gets `EVar("Unit")` for a body.

## Core.kt { #core-kt }

The tree FieldML actually evaluates: the typed tree with its source positions dropped and its
multi-parameter lambdas curried into one-parameter [`CLam`](languages.md#core-kt-clam) nodes.

[`Lowerer`](languages.md#lowerer-kt-lowerer) is the only thing that builds one and [`Evaluator`](languages.md#evaluator-kt-evaluator) the only thing that walks one. Every
case here corresponds to a case of the typed tree, and the lowering is a case-for-case mapping
apart from the lambda, so the two hierarchies are easy to read side by side.

What the lowering leaves behind is as informative as what it keeps. Types stay on every node, so a
later pass can still ask what a subexpression is. Ranges do not, so an evaluation failure carries
no position of its own, and a box reports it against the fragment that was run rather than the
subexpression that failed. [`CLet`](languages.md#core-kt-clet) keeps the `recursive` flag but has no parameter list, because by
this point a `let f x = ...`'s parameters are the lambda sitting in its `value`.
[`CoreConstructor`](languages.md#core-kt-coreconstructor) keeps a constructor's name and arity and drops its type scheme, which has
already done its work in inference.

## Evaluator.kt { #evaluator-kt }

The FieldML runtime: it walks a lowered [`CoreExpr`](languages.md#core-kt-coreexpr) tree and returns the [`FieldMLValue`](languages.md#evaluator-kt-fieldmlvalue) the tree
evaluates to.

This is the last stage of the pipeline. [`Lowerer`](languages.md#lowerer-kt-lowerer) hands over a tree whose lambdas are already
curried and whose source ranges are already gone, so nothing here can report a position and a
box blames the fragment it ran rather than the subexpression that failed. An [`Evaluator`](languages.md#evaluator-kt-evaluator) holds
the prelude it was constructed with and builds a fresh root scope for every `evaluate`, so two
runs of the same box share no state.

Most of the value shapes are what their names say. Two are not. `HostValue` wraps an arbitrary
JVM object, which is how a FieldML box reaches Field at all: [`FieldMLHostBridge`](languages.md#hostbridge-kt-fieldmlhostbridge) both produces
and consumes these, and `Vec2`, `Vec3` and `Vec4` are `HostValue`s holding the mutable linalg
vector types rather than a FieldML shape of their own. Arithmetic on them and access to their
`x`, `y`, `z` and `w` components are therefore special-cased here, component-wise between
vectors of equal width and broadcast against a scalar, and always into a freshly allocated
vector, because the linalg types are mutable and a FieldML value is not. `FactoryValue` is the
other: [`RuntimeEnv`](languages.md#evaluator-kt-runtimeenv) calls its `create` on every lookup, so each mention of the name is a
separate value while a `let`-bound name is one value. The prelude uses this once, for `fline`,
and needs to, because `moveTo` and `lineTo` mutate the line they are handed and return it.

`hostToFieldMLValue` and `fieldMLValueToHost` are the conversion pair at the JVM boundary, and
they are not inverses. A tuple leaves as a plain `List` and comes back a list, so a round trip
through the host loses the distinction the type checker made; records, unit and the numeric
shapes survive one. Closures, native functions, partially applied constructors and ADT values
leave as themselves rather than as anything JVM-shaped, which is what lets the bridge's SAM
proxy apply one later.

Scope is a chain of [`RuntimeEnv`](languages.md#evaluator-kt-runtimeenv)s with one parent each. A `let` always makes a child; a
recursive one evaluates its own body in the scope that will hold the name, and a plain one
evaluates in the parent, so `let x = x + 1` reads the outer `x`. A match makes one child per
case it tries, and a value matching no case fails at this point: nothing earlier checks
exhaustiveness, and this runtime error is the only mention of it in FieldML.

Two failures here have their cause somewhere else. The walk is directly recursive with no
trampoline, so deep FieldML recursion arrives as a JVM `StackOverflowError` and not as a FieldML
diagnostic. And an unknown runtime name means the two halves of the prelude have drifted apart:
[`Inferencer`](languages.md#inferencer-kt-inferencer) already rejects any name `FieldMLTypePrelude.schemes` does not list, so a name that
type-checked and then went missing is one `FieldMLRuntimePrelude.values` does not define.

## HostBridge.kt { #hostbridge-kt }

How a FieldML box calls Kotlin: `hostCall`, `hostNew` and `hostGet` all arrive here, and so does
a `.field` read on a host value.

FieldML has no declarations for Field's API and no generated stubs for it. A box names a method
with a string, and all of the matching happens at run time against `java.lang.reflect`. That
leaves this file three problems a compiled language would have settled at its own compile time:
choosing between same-named overloads, giving a FieldML function a JVM type it can be passed
as, and reconciling FieldML's one integer and one float with the JVM's six numeric widths. The
`object` below takes them in that order.

[`FieldMLHostTypes`](languages.md#hosttypes-kt-fieldmlhosttypes) answers the same three questions a second time, because typing a `hostCall`
means predicting which member this file will pick. Where the answer is a judgement rather than a
lookup the two share one implementation rather than agreeing twice: `numericAffinity` scores
numeric fit for both, and both read a wildcard from the bound that carries the information for
the position it appears in. When they drift, a box type-checks and then invokes the wrong member,
which is a harder failure to read than either a type error or a refusal.

`dev_docs/FIELDML_HOST_BRIDGE.md` is the longer account, including the named-argument mechanisms
that make Kotlin's default parameters reachable from FieldML at all.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/fieldml/core/HostBridge.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/fieldml/core/HostBridge/)

## Lowerer.kt { #lowerer-kt }

The last stage of the FieldML front end: the typed tree becomes the [`CoreExpr`](languages.md#core-kt-coreexpr) tree the evaluator
walks.

Almost all of it is a rename. Each case of the typed tree has one case in the core tree, the
inferred type is copied across, and the source range is dropped. Two things inference needed go
no further: a `let`'s parameter list, which by this point is the lambda sitting in its value,
and a constructor's type scheme, which reduces to the name and arity [`CoreConstructor`](languages.md#core-kt-coreconstructor) keeps.

The one real transformation is currying. A lambda written `fun x y -> ...` becomes two nested
one-parameter [`CLam`](languages.md#core-kt-clam) nodes, so the evaluator only ever binds one parameter at a time. Each of
those nodes carries its own type and they are different types: the outer node's is the whole
arrow, the inner node's is the arrow that starts at the second parameter. So the lowering walks
the arrow outside in, one step per parameter, keeping the type each parameter starts from, and
then builds the nodes from the innermost parameter back out.

Nothing here reports anything. A tree that reaches this stage has already been typed, so there is
no result to check: [`FieldMLCompiler`](languages.md#fieldmlcompiler-kt-fieldmlcompiler) runs the lowerer and returns what comes back.

## Diagnostics.kt { #diagnostics-kt }

Where a FieldML compile says something is wrong, and how badly.

This is the package the rest of the front end shares, and the only one that depends on nothing:
the lexer, the parser, the inferencer and the lowerer all import it, and it imports none of them.
A stage with something to report either adds a [`Diagnostic`](languages.md#diagnostics-kt-diagnostic) to the list it returns or, where
carrying on would mean inventing a tree, throws [`CompileAbort`](languages.md#diagnostics-kt-compileabort) and lets its own entry point turn
that back into a diagnostic.

Only an error stops a compile. Each stage runs if no earlier diagnostic was an error, so a
[`Severity`](languages.md#diagnostics-kt-severity) of `Warning` or `Info` is collected and reported without holding the run up.

Nothing outside `afield.lang.fieldml` imports these types. They leave the front end inside
`CompilationResult`, and the box runtime reads them from there to put a message on a line.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/fieldml/diag/Diagnostics.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/fieldml/diag/Diagnostics/)

## Lexer.kt { #lexer-kt }

FieldML's first stage: source text in, a flat list of [`Token`](languages.md#token-kt-token)s out, and a diagnostic for anything
that could not be read.

The scan never stops early. A character the lexer cannot use costs one diagnostic and no token,
and the scan carries on, so a typo halfway down a box does not hide what is below it. Whether the
*compile* carries on is a separate decision, made by `FieldMLCompiler`, which does not reach the
parser at all once lexing has reported an error.

Trivia is skipped rather than emitted: `//` to the end of the line, and `(* … *)` blocks, which
nest by depth count, so a region commented out this way can contain comments of its own. An
unterminated block is reported at the position it was opened.

The shapes a literal can take are all decided here. A number is digits, and a `.` opens a
fraction only when a digit follows it, which leaves `.` free to be the field-access token and
makes `1.` an `INT` and then a `DOT`; there is no exponent form, and a leading `-` is always a
token of its own rather than part of the literal. An identifier starts with a letter or `_` and
may carry `'` after that. A string runs to the next unescaped `"`, and one that reaches the end
of the source first is reported rather than closed. `&`, `:` and `!` are errors on their own,
since only `&&`, `::` and `!=` exist, and the first two say so in the message.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/fieldml/lex/Lexer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/fieldml/lex/Lexer/)

## Token.kt { #token-kt }

One [`TokenKind`](languages.md#token-kt-tokenkind) for every lexeme FieldML has, and the [`Token`](languages.md#token-kt-token) that pairs a kind with the text it
was read from.

There is no kind for whitespace or for a comment: the lexer skips trivia instead of emitting it,
so a token list cannot be printed back as the source it came from. Keywords are kinds of their
own rather than identifiers with reserved text, which is what lets the parser ask for `LET` or
`WITH` by kind, and also what stops those words being used as names.

## Parser.kt { #parser-kt }

FieldML's second stage: tokens in, the surface tree out, by recursive descent with precedence
climbing for the operators.

There is no error recovery. The first token the parser cannot use throws, [`parse`](languages.md#parser-kt--parser--parse) catches it, and
the result is no tree and exactly one diagnostic. Where the lexer reports every character it
could not read, the parser reports only the first thing it could not fit into the grammar.

Two places in the grammar are settled by columns rather than by tokens, and they are what lets a
box be written as a stack of bindings with no `in` and a record as a block with no separators.
The value of a top-level `let` ends at the next line that starts no further right than the `let`
itself, so a continuation has to be indented. A record field's value ends at `}`, at a `,` or
`;`, or at the next `name =` that starts a later line. Both are carried down into the expression
parser as predicates, so they apply at whatever depth the expression has reached rather than only
at the top.

Function application binds tighter than every operator, and prefix `-` binds looser than
application, so `-f x` negates the call. `::` is the one right-associative operator. `|>` gets no
node of its own: `a |> f` is parsed as the call `f a`, which is why nothing after this stage has a
case for a pipe.

A program is a chain of `let` and `type` declarations ending in an expression. One that ends on a
binding instead evaluates to `Unit`, and a `type` declaration with nothing after it is an error
rather than a program.

## FieldMLTypePrelude.kt { #fieldmltypeprelude-kt }

The type of every name a FieldML program has before it declares anything: the prelude, as the
type checker sees it.

[`schemes`](languages.md#fieldmltypeprelude-kt--fieldmltypeprelude--schemes) is the root environment `Inferencer` starts from, so a name here is in scope in every
FieldML box. Each entry is a [`Scheme`](languages.md#types-kt-scheme) rather than a bare type, because most of the prelude is
polymorphic and a bare type cannot say *how* polymorphic: `map` works over any element type,
`abs` over `Int` or `Float` but not over a string, `dot` over two vectors as long as they are
the same width. A scheme carries those restrictions on its quantified variables, which is what
lets one entry stand in for what would otherwise be a pile of overloads.

`FieldMLRuntimePrelude` holds the other half, name for name: the values these types describe.
The two lists are matched by hand and nothing in the build compares them. What the build does
guard is the page a reader looks the prelude up in, through
`FieldMLCheatsheetCoverageTest.everyPreludeNameIsListedWithItsType`, which fails when a name is
added, removed or retyped without `public/docs/fieldml_cheatsheet.md` following.

The [`THost`](languages.md#types-kt-thost) values at the top are the handful of host types FieldML names. Everything else the
JVM offers arrives as the opaque `Host`, and the `host…` family of intrinsics is how a program
says what a value of that type actually is.

## HostTypes.kt { #hosttypes-kt }

The reflection behind FieldML's host types: what a [`THost`](languages.md#types-kt-thost) names, and what can therefore be said
at type-check time about a member's type, a resolved overload's result, the parameter slots a
call's arguments land in, and the members a receiver actually has.

A [`THost`](languages.md#types-kt-thost)'s name is a real JVM class name, which is what keeps a program typed once it reaches
into the JVM: a member access is inferred rather than left dynamic, a misspelled member name is
reported where it is written instead of crashing on the first run, and completion has a class to
enumerate.

Two rules bound what this file will claim.

*`Host` stays the dynamic type.* `OPAQUE`, the name `Host` itself, is what a host type degrades to
whenever reflection cannot justify anything better: a generic erased to `Object`, an array, a
`Map`, a nullable return, an overload set whose best candidates disagree about what they return.
`Inferencer.unifyHosts` lets it stand for any class, which is the statement "unknown, checked at
run time". It is a *bounded* dynamic type rather than a universal one, though:
`Inferencer.requireDynamicallyReachable` refuses a `Host` where a function, a list, a tuple or a
record is wanted, and names what to reach for instead.

*A mapping only claims what the runtime actually does.* `fieldMLTypeOf` answers with the type
`afield.lang.fieldml.core.hostToFieldMLValue` will really produce, so reflection saying `int` means an
`IntValue` arrives, and `List<Double>` means a list of floats. Where the declared type does not
determine the converted one the answer is `Host` rather than something plausible: a `Map` really
does convert to a record, but its field names are nowhere in the declared type, so the type side
says `Host` and the program reads the fields with `hostGet`.

## Inferencer.kt { #inferencer-kt }

FieldML's type checker: a Hindley-Milner inference pass over the surface tree, producing the
typed tree the lowerer consumes.

The core of it is the textbook algorithm. Every unknown is a numbered type variable; unification
makes two types equal by binding variables in one substitution the whole run shares; pruning
follows a bound variable to what it stands for and shortens the chain behind it; an occurs check
refuses a type that would contain itself. A `let` generalizes over the variables its value has
and its environment does not, so each use of a bound name instantiates that scheme with fresh
variables.

Three things here are not the textbook's:

- **A host type carries a JVM class.** Two of them unify when either class is assignable from the
  other, because Field's own signatures mix a writable class with its read-only interface. The
  bare `Host` is the dynamic escape, and a bounded one: it stands for a value whose class is
  unknown rather than one whose shape is unknown, so it unifies with a number, a string, a
  boolean or another object, and refuses a function, a list, a tuple or a record.
- **A saturated `host…` call is typed by reflection rather than by a scheme.** What `hostGet`
  returns depends on the text of a string and the class of a receiver, which no one scheme can
  state, so the member is looked up and the call is either typed or refused where it was written
  instead of at the first run. A program that shadows the intrinsic is left alone. Curried
  application is left-nested, so the ordinary walk would reach a lambda argument before the
  receiver that says what its parameters are; a host call's spine is inferred ahead of that walk
  to put the order right, which is how a callback written as a positional argument gets its
  parameter types from the receiver's class.
- **Numeric and vector type variables are constrained**, which is as much of a class system as
  FieldML has. A variable that has been through a numeric or vector requirement is recorded as
  such, the requirement is rechecked at the moment the variable is bound, and one that is still
  a variable when the tree is finalized is defaulted: `Float` for numeric, `Vec2` for vector.

Every failure leaves through the same abort, which throws rather than returning, so an
[`InferResult`](languages.md#inferencer-kt-inferresult) either carries a typed tree and no diagnostics at all, or no tree and exactly one
error.

## TypedAst.kt { #typedast-kt }

FieldML's syntax tree after inference: the same shape as the surface tree in `afield.lang.fieldml.ast`, with
a [`Type`](languages.md#types-kt-type) on every expression and on every pattern.

[`Inferencer`](languages.md#inferencer-kt-inferencer) produces it and [`Lowerer`](languages.md#lowerer-kt-lowerer) consumes it. Source ranges survive inference, which is what
lets a type error point at the text that caused it, and this is the last stage to have them: the
`afield.lang.fieldml.core` tree the evaluator runs keeps the types and drops the positions.

Three things here are inference's findings rather than a restatement of the syntax:

  - `TExprLet.recursive` is true for the `let f x = ...` function form, which is the form whose
    own name is in scope inside its body.
  - `TExprLet.parameters` repeats the parameters of the lambda that the binding's value became,
    and is empty when the value is not a lambda.
  - [`TypedConstructor`](languages.md#typedast-kt-typedconstructor) gives each constructor of a declared data type its arity and the [`Scheme`](languages.md#types-kt-scheme)
    its name was bound under, so `Some` is an ordinary curried function from there on.

`walkTyped` is the one walker over the hierarchy, and completion is its caller: it compiles a
probe program and looks for the [`TExprLambda`](languages.md#typedast-kt-texprlambda) whose parameter names match the lambda under the
caret, which is how a callback's parameters have types before a reader has written any.

## Types.kt { #types-kt }

The types FieldML infers, and the two ways one is printed back to a reader.

[`Type`](languages.md#types-kt-type) is the vocabulary inference works in: five ground types, a unification variable [`TVar`](languages.md#types-kt-tvar), an
arrow [`TFun`](languages.md#types-kt-tfun), the structural cases [`TRecord`](languages.md#types-kt-trecord), [`TTuple`](languages.md#types-kt-ttuple) and [`TList`](languages.md#types-kt-tlist), [`TAdt`](languages.md#types-kt-tadt) for a declared data
type applied to its arguments, and [`THost`](languages.md#types-kt-thost) for a JVM type reached over the host bridge, whose
`name` is what `FieldMLHostTypes` reflects on. [`TFun`](languages.md#types-kt-tfun) takes one argument at a time, matching the
curried application the parser builds, so a function of two arguments is `TFun(a, TFun(b, c))`.

A [`Scheme`](languages.md#types-kt-scheme) is a type together with the variable ids generalised over it, and it can restrict what
those ids are allowed to become. An id listed in `numeric` only unifies with `Int` or `Float`, and
one listed in `vector` only with `Vec2`, `Vec3` or `Vec4`. That is how the prelude gives `abs`,
`min`, `max` and `clamp` one scheme each rather than one per numeric type, and `dot`, `vlength`,
`normalize` and `mix` one each rather than one per vector width.

[`TypePrinter`](languages.md#types-kt-typeprinter) renders a type two ways. `print` parenthesises every arrow, and is what diagnostics
and a box's inline result use; `printSignature` drops the parentheses that right associativity
makes redundant, and is what completion shows and what the cheatsheet's coverage guard compares
against. A printer names unification variables `'a`, `'b`, … in order of first appearance and
keeps those names for its own lifetime, so two types printed by one printer agree about which
variable is which, while two printers each start again at `'a`.

## ForthInterface.kt { #forthinterface-kt }

Makes ForthField a language a box can be written in.

`ForthInterpreter.kt` is the language itself. This file is the half that joins it to the
workspace: the `BoxExecution` a ForthField box runs under, and the registration that puts
"Set Main Language: ForthField" in front of a user.

### Running code

[`ForthExecution`](languages.md#forthinterface-kt-forthexecution) answers the execution contract a box's editor talks to. Running a fragment,
or the whole box, evaluates the source once and reports each diagnostic on the line that produced
it, printing `ok` — with what the run left on the stack, the top value in bold — when a run
finished cleanly and produced no visible output of its own.
Completion offers the dictionary's words, each with the kind and the documentation the
interpreter holds for it. Executing a symbol runs one named word as a single-line fragment.

Launching is the one that is more than an evaluation. The code runs once to define its words, and
if its last token names a colon definition, that word becomes a *strand*: a coroutine that
re-executes it until the box's run generation for that strand moves on, yielding between passes.
`frame` is available only there, and it ends a pass rather than the strand, so a word can be
written as the body of a per-frame loop. Anything else the code ends with defines words and stops.
Stopping the box cancels every strand job and bumps every run generation.

### Becoming a ForthField box

A box does not choose this language for itself; its parent does. `installForth` registers a
`MainLanguageRuntime` under the id `forth`, and makes the `isForthRoot` flag one of the
properties a document persists. `installForthPlugin` starts a `TopologyWatcher`, and
`forthTopologyNeedsUpdating` is what that watcher calls on every graph edit: each child of a box
flagged `isForthRoot`, or set to the `forth` main language, is given a `ForthExecution`, and a
child left with no such parent goes back to Kotlin. Each child gets an interpreter of its own, so
a stack and a dictionary belong to one box and outlive the run that filled them.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/forth/ForthInterface.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/forth/ForthInterface/)

## ForthInterpreter.kt { #forthinterpreter-kt }

ForthField — a compact, extensible Forth used by Field4 for live coding.

It is host-driven:
- it executes ForthField source and keeps its own data stack/dictionary
- it ships with creative-coding oriented builtins (vectors + [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline))
- it can be extended at runtime from Kotlin via [`defineWord`](languages.md#forthinterpreter-kt--forthinterpreter--defineword)
- it can interoperate with host objects using `@?` / `@?!` reflection calls

### The host loop

Typical host loop:
1. Construct an interpreter once (`val forth = ForthInterpreter()`).
2. Register host bridge words with [`defineWord`](languages.md#forthinterpreter-kt--forthinterpreter--defineword) as needed.
3. Push host objects (buffers, context values, services) onto [`stack`](languages.md#forthinterpreter-kt--forthinterpreter--stack).
4. Run `eval(...)`.
5. Pop resulting values (for example an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)) and hand them to rendering/output code.

Example: basic execution and stack access:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val forth = ForthInterpreter()
val diagnostics = forth.eval("2 3 +")
check(diagnostics.isEmpty())
println(forth.popNum()) // 5.0
```

Example: defining words in ForthField:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: sqr ( n -- n2 ) dup * ;
: hypot2 ( x y -- d2 ) sqr swap sqr + ;
3 4 hypot2 .
```

Example: create an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) shape in ForthField:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: stroke-ribbon ( -- f )
  fline
  0   0   moveto
  120 20  lineto
  160 90  210 90  260 20 cubicto
  320 0   lineto
  true  fline-stroked
  false fline-filled
  1.0 0.55 0.2 1.0 fline-color
  2.5 fline-thickness ;

stroke-ribbon
```

Host-side consumption of the resulting [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline):
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val forth = ForthInterpreter()
val source = """
  : stroke-ribbon ( -- f )
    fline
    0 0 moveto
    120 20 lineto
    160 90 210 90 260 20 cubicto
    true fline-stroked
    1 0.55 0.2 1 fline-color
    2.5 fline-thickness ;
  stroke-ribbon
""".trimIndent()

val diagnostics = forth.eval(source)
if (diagnostics.isEmpty()) {
  val line = forth.pop() as FLine
  // Forward `line` into your output channel / renderer.
}
```

Example: use vector helpers with FLine convenience words:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: zig ( -- f )
  fline
  0   0   vec2 fline-moveto-v2
  40  20  vec2 fline-lineto-v2
  80 -10  vec2 fline-lineto-v2
  120 25  vec2 fline-lineto-v2
  1 0 0 1 fline-node-color ;
zig
```

### The reflection bridge

Example: resolve classes without full FQNs.
`class-for` consults Field's class cache (`importHelp.kt`) so short names usually work.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
s"FLine" class-for @? getName println
s"Vec3"  class-for @? getName println

s"Fli" class-matches print   \ returns a list of FQNs
s"Fli" class-help            \ prints one-per-line suggestions
```

Example: reflection bridge (`@?` / `@?!`) with [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline), built entirely by class lookup.
This demonstrates construction + method calls without using the `fline` helper.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable f
s"FLine" class-for @? newInstance f !

\ Explicit arity call: f.moveTo(Number, Number, Number)
f @ 0   0   0   3 @?! moveTo drop

\ Explicit arity call: f.lineTo(Number, Number, Number)
f @ 120 30  0   3 @?! lineTo drop
f @ 220 10  0   3 @?! lineTo drop
f @ 260 80 0  320 80 0  380 20 0  9 @?! cubicTo drop

\ Properties are just a map on FLine
f @ @? properties  s"thickness" 2.5 2 @?! put
f @ @? properties  s"stroked" true 2 @?! put

\ Heuristic call for zero-arg methods works well with @?
f @ @? close drop

\ Leave the final FLine on the stack
f @
```

Example: `@?` reads data too (field/getter/method fallback):
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
f @ @? nodes   \ push internal node list
@? size .      \ call size() on that list and print node count
```

Example: constructor with explicit args via `@?! new`:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable sb
s"StringBuilder" class-for s"hello" 1 @?! new sb !
sb @ @? toString println
```

Example: extending ForthField with Kotlin bridge words.
Here we expose a helper that appends a `vec4` worth of floats into any
`DynamicallyWriteable` buffer (for example `VulkanBuffer` or `FrameBufferGroup`).

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
import afield.graphics.vulkan.buffers.DynamicallyWriteable
import afield.math.linalg.Vec4

val forth = ForthInterpreter()
forth.defineWord("append-vec4", "( buf x y z w -- buf )") {
  val w = popNum().toFloat()
  val z = popNum().toFloat()
  val y = popNum().toFloat()
  val x = popNum().toFloat()
  val buf = pop() as DynamicallyWriteable

  buf.append {
    put(Vec4(x, y, z, w))
  }
  push(buf)
}
```

Example: call that bridge word from ForthField after pushing a host buffer:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
forth.push(myDynamicBuffer) // host object: VulkanBuffer / FrameBufferGroup / similar
forth.eval("""
  0.0 1.0 0.0 1.0 append-vec4
  1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 append-vec4
  0.0 0.0 1.0 1.0 append-vec4
""".trimIndent())
```

Example: long-form output areas from ForthField:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
s"<b>Inline-ish output area content</b>" html
s"<pre>Detailed log text...</pre>" s"debug" html-channel
```

Example: launchable animation with cooperative yielding via `frame`.
Run this in Launch mode (or call `begin("default")` on the box), so `spinner` executes
every RunLoop tick. `frame` yields immediately, letting the rest of Field proceed.
Store evolving state in variables, because each strand tick re-enters the word from the top.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable tick
variable line
0 tick !

: spinner ( -- )
  s"FLine" class-for @? newInstance line !

  \ center point
  line @ 0 0 0 3 @?! moveTo drop

  \ animated endpoint (simple circular motion)
  line @
  tick @ 0.05 * dup cos 120 *          ( x )
             swap sin 120 *            ( x y )
  0 3 @?! lineTo drop

  \ style via reflected property map
  line @ @? properties s"thickness" 2.0 2 @?! put
  line @ @? properties s"stroked" true 2 @?! put
  line @ s"geom" display-channel

  \ show a debug line in output area
  s"tick=" tick @ str str+ s"debug" display-channel

  1 tick +!
  frame
;

spinner
```

Example: same pattern with an explicit ForthField loop.
`frame` exits the current tick immediately; on next tick the word starts again.

```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable phase
0 phase !

: pulse-loop ( -- )
  begin
    s"phase=" phase @ str str+ println
    1 phase +!
    frame
  again ;

pulse-loop
```

Example: full overwrite of float data each tick, since `write` replaces the payload rather than
adding to it:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
import afield.graphics.vulkan.buffers.DynamicallyWriteable

forth.defineWord("write-triangle", "( buf -- buf )") {
  val buf = pop() as DynamicallyWriteable
  buf.write {
    // XYZW packed per vertex (3 vertices)
    put(-0.5f); put(-0.5f); put(0f); put(1f)
    put( 0.5f); put(-0.5f); put(0f); put(1f)
    put( 0.0f); put( 0.5f); put(0f); put(1f)
  }
  push(buf)
}
```

Notes for dynamic-buffer bridging:
- [`defineWord`](languages.md#forthinterpreter-kt--forthinterpreter--defineword) closures execute on the interpreter thread/context used by your host.
- Prefer `write { ... }` when replacing the payload; `append { ... }` when accumulating.
- `DynamicBuffer.put(Vec4)` follows std430-friendly alignment rules used by Field's buffer code.
- If you need explicit control, call `putScalar(...)` repeatedly instead of vector helpers.

### Builtins

Builtins included by default:
- stack ops (`dup`, `swap`, `over`, `pick`, `roll`, ...)
- math/logic/control flow (`if/else/then`, `begin/until`, `do/loop`, ...)
- variables/constants (`variable`, `!`, `@`, `constant`)
- strings/output (`."..."`, `s"..."`, `.`, `println`, ...)
- dictionary tools (`words`, `see`, `forget`, `recurse`)
- return-stack transfer (`>r`, `r>`, `r@`)
- vectors (`vec2`, `vec3`, `vec4` + arithmetic helpers)
- [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) primitives (`fline`, `moveto`, `lineto`, `cubicto`, styling words)
- small visualization words (`html`, `watch`, `stack-display`, `bar`, `plot-stack`)
- frame/yield primitive (`frame`) for cooperative launch-mode animations
- host reflection hooks (`@?`, `@?!`, `class-for`, `class-matches`, `class-help`)

### Dictionary, recursion and the return stack

Dictionary / debugging examples:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: sqr dup * ;
words              \ print all currently known words
see sqr            \ print ": sqr dup * ;"
forget sqr         \ remove the user-defined word
```

Recursion example:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: countdown ( n -- )
  dup 0> if
    dup println
    1- recurse
  else
    drop
  then ;
5 countdown
```

Infinite loop example. Use `again` mainly in launched words where `frame`
yields back to Field each tick:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
variable tick
: ticker begin tick @ println 1 tick +! frame again ;
ticker
```

Return-stack examples. `>r` moves a temporary value away from the data stack,
`r@` copies it back, and `r>` restores/removes it:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
: add-twice ( a b -- a+b+b )
  >r        \ return stack: b ; data stack: a
  r@ +      \ data stack: a+b, b is still saved
  r> + ;    \ data stack: a+b+b
```

### Visualization words

Visualization examples:
```diffstatic {data-lang=forth}
s"<b>Hello from Forth</b>" html
0.72 1.0 s"progress" bar
42 s"answer" watch
stack-display
1 4 9 16 plot-stack
```

## MorphoCircuit.kt { #morphocircuit-kt }

The grow-and-draw handle: a compiled MorphoHDL circuit that expands a few cells per frame while
its layout relaxes between expansions.

`MorphoCircuit.compile` takes a design name and a bus signature and returns something compiled
but not yet expanded. `step` is shaped to be the condition of a run loop, so the recursive
division is watchable rather than already finished; `growFully` is the same circuit with the
watching skipped. Either way the current [`MorphoNetlist`](languages.md#morphonetlist-kt-morphonetlist) and [`MorphoTiming`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphotiming) are readable between
steps, which is what lets a neighbouring Kotlin box draw a half-built circuit.

A morpho box publishes one of these on `Box.morphoCircuit`; a Kotlin box builds its own with
`morphoCircuit(...)` from `MorphoFLines.kt`. It holds a guest-side session and a WASM layout, so
it has to be closed.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoCircuit.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoCircuit/)

## MorphoFLines.kt { #morphoflines-kt }

Drawing a MorphoHDL circuit with Field's FLines.

This is the half of the bridge morpho does not supply and Field does. Upstream renders with
SwissGL and a Canvas 2D fallback (`viewer.js`, `layout_renderer.js`, `bloom.js` — about 1,900
lines), none of which is vendored. Field already draws graphs, so a circuit becomes one FLine
per wire and one point-set per gate, and everything downstream — SVG export, the plane grid,
animation, the docs capture pipeline — comes along for free.

### Colour carries the simulation

By default wires are coloured by **signal arrival time**, which is what makes the picture worth
looking at rather than a hairball: the inputs are one end of the ramp, the critical path is the
other, and the difference between a ripple adder and a Brent–Kung is visible as a gradient
rather than inferable from a gate count.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoFLines.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoFLines/)

**Used in:** [MorphoHDL in Field](../morpho_examples.md), [Searching for MorphoHDL Circuits](../morpho_search.md)

## MorphoGenerator.kt { #morphogenerator-kt }

Where MorphoHDL programs come from when nobody writes them.

A sketch fixes everything about a cell that the search is *not* looking for — its name, its
ports, what it falls back into — and leaves the body open. That split is deliberate: "find a
circuit" with nothing fixed is a search over parse errors, and the interesting question is not
whether a random walk can discover the token `def`.

### Repair rather than reject

Mutation operators here are allowed to produce nonsense, and [`MorphoProgramGenerator.repair`](languages.md#morphogenerator-kt--morphoprogramgenerator--repair)
projects it back into the region the width model calls plausible: an argument that names a wire
out of scope is rewired, a `SPLIT` of a one-bit bus is deleted, a recursive call that would not
narrow has its arguments resampled. Rejection-and-resample would be simpler and much worse —
with a rejection rate near one the search stops being a search.

The compiler still has the last word. Repair only makes candidates *likely* to compile; the
fraction that does not is reported as [`MorphoSearchRun.failureRate`](languages.md#morphosearch-kt--morphosearchrun--failurerate) rather than hidden.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoGenerator.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoGenerator/)

## MorphoGenome.kt { #morphogenome-kt }

The thing a search actually mutates: a MorphoHDL **program, as text**.

A generator could build netlists directly and skip the compiler, and it would be faster. It
would also optimise against Field's idea of what morpho compiles a design into rather than
against MorphoHDL. So a genome renders to source, upstream's `parse()` reads it, upstream's
`compileModule()` compiles it, and anything the search finds can be pasted into a morpho box and
will still be there tomorrow.

### The grammar this has to hit

`parser.js` is 190 lines and its accepted language is small (`parser.js:23-188`):

* top-level `Name = LUT(arity, value)`;
* `@morpho` or `@morpho(fallback=X)`, then `def name(a, b, c):`;
* SSA lines `t0, t1 = OP(x, y)`, one per line;
* `return x, y`.

That is all [`MorphoGenome.render`](languages.md#morphogenome-kt--morphogenome--render) emits, and it is why the rendered text is legible: it is not a
serialisation format, it is the language.

### Where the widths come from

MorphoHDL infers bus widths and never declares them, so a generator that ignores widths produces
mostly-invalid programs. [`MorphoWidthModel`](languages.md#morphogenome-kt-morphowidthmodel) is Field's *model* of that inference — it mirrors
`primitives.js`'s `SPLIT`/`CAT` and `compiler.js`'s `materializeLut` broadcast rule — and it is
used only to steer generation. The compiler remains the judge; the model's accuracy shows up as
[`MorphoSearchRun.failureRate`](languages.md#morphosearch-kt--morphosearchrun--failurerate) and nowhere else.

## MorphoGraal.kt { #morphograal-kt }

Hosting MorphoHDL's own compiler: one GraalJS context, one lock, and a growth handle per circuit.

Nothing about the language is reimplemented on this side. [`MorphoRuntime`](languages.md#morphograal-kt-morphoruntime) evaluates morpho's
parser, compiler and expansion as ES modules, at the upstream commit recorded in
`morpho/PROVENANCE.md`, and [`MorphoSession`](languages.md#morphograal-kt-morphosession) holds one compiled design that is expanded a budget
at a time. The rest of the package consumes what comes back out: [`MorphoNetlist`](languages.md#morphonetlist-kt-morphonetlist) is the
snapshot, [`MorphoSim`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphosim) evaluates it, [`MorphoLayout3D`](languages.md#morpholayout3d-kt-morpholayout3d) places it, `MorphoFLines.kt` draws it.

Crossing the boundary is the expensive part, so both guest scripts exist to make each crossing
carry more. `morpho-field-driver.mjs` flattens the compiler's graph into typed arrays;
`morpho-field-layout.mjs` drives the Barnes–Hut kernel from JavaScript, where its buffers can be
wrapped in views rather than read an element at a time. A guest failure arrives as
[`MorphoException`](languages.md#morphograal-kt-morphoexception), carrying morpho's own source line whenever its parser supplied one.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoGraal.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoGraal/)

## MorphoInterface.kt { #morphointerface-kt }

Field4 language adapter for MorphoHDL, a Python-syntax hardware-description language.

MorphoHDL programs describe recursive circuit structures that Field compiles via morpho's
own compiler on GraalJS and lays out with its Barnes–Hut kernel on GraalWasm. The result
lands on [`Box.morphoCircuit`](languages.md#morphointerface-kt--morphocircuit); a neighbouring Kotlin box reads it and draws with
`circuit.flines()`.

[`MorphoExecution`](languages.md#morphointerface-kt-morphoexecution) is the [`BoxExecution`](workspace.md#execution-kt-boxexecution) implementation. Setting a parent box's `isMorphoRoot`
to `true` turns its children into MorphoHDL boxes. Execute mode grows the circuit to
completion; launch mode expands a few cells per frame while relaxing the layout between
expansions, so the recursive division is visible in motion. [`installMorpho`](languages.md#morphointerface-kt--installmorpho) registers the
runtime; [`installMorphoPlugin`](languages.md#morphointerface-kt--installmorphoplugin) starts the topology watcher.

## MorphoLayout3D.kt { #morpholayout3d-kt }

Placement for a MorphoHDL circuit: every active cell gets a 3D position, from a force-directed
layout running on morpho's own Barnes–Hut kernel.

One of the two things Field does with a [`MorphoNetlist`](languages.md#morphonetlist-kt-morphonetlist) snapshot, the other being [`MorphoSim`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphosim);
`MorphoFLines.kt` turns the positions that come out of here into `FLine`s. Layout is stepped
alongside growth rather than run to convergence at the end, and a cell born in a growth step is
seeded at its parent's position, so a circuit that is still expanding is drawable on every frame.

The parameters are upstream's defaults, and the only behavioural difference from morpho's own
demo is that Field leaves the z axis free.

## MorphoNetlist.kt { #morphonetlist-kt }

The compiled circuit as a Kotlin value: packed per-cell metadata, one array per relation, and
morpho's own numbering carried across the boundary unchanged.

`MorphoSession.netlist` builds one of these out of the GraalJS guest in a handful of bulk copies,
and everything Field does with a circuit reads it from here: [`MorphoSim`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphosim) evaluates it,
[`MorphoLayout3D`](languages.md#morpholayout3d-kt-morpholayout3d) places it, `MorphoFLines.kt` draws it. It is a snapshot rather than a view, so
growing the circuit produces a new one.

Cell indices are morpho's, so deactivated cells are still counted and `isActive` decides what is
real. A LUT cell is broadcast across a bus, so the count of active cells, the count of LUTs and
the count of gates are three different numbers.

## MorphoProblems.kt { #morphoproblems-kt }

The search problems this layer was built to ask, and how much of the answer each one gives away.

Each one is a [`MorphoSpec`](languages.md#morphospec-kt-morphospec) (what the circuit must compute, at which widths) plus a
[`MorphoProgramGenerator`](languages.md#morphogenerator-kt-morphoprogramgenerator) (what a candidate is allowed to be). They live here rather than inside
a test, so a Field box, the measurement run and the regression tests all ask the same question,
and a number quoted in the documentation is a number an assertion also checks.

They range from `bitwiseXor`, where one broadcast LUT is enough and a failure implicates the
harness rather than the search, through `fullAdderCell`'s eight-vector exhaustive truth table, to
`adderFromScratch`, where the recursion and the base case it falls into are evolved together and
nothing about addition is supplied but the oracle.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoProblems.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoProblems/)

## MorphoSearch.kt { #morphosearch-kt }

Searching the space of MorphoHDL programs for one that computes something.

Three drivers, one evaluator, one generator. That is the arrangement the whole file exists for:
[`MorphoSearch.random`](languages.md#morphosearch-kt--morphosearch--random) is a **control arm** drawing from exactly the distribution
[`MorphoSearch.hillClimb`](languages.md#morphosearch-kt--morphosearch--hillclimb) and [`MorphoSearch.evolve`](languages.md#morphosearch-kt--morphosearch--evolve) mutate within, so a difference between their
results is a difference in *selection*. Reporting an evolutionary result without the control next
to it would say nothing at all — a generator good enough to make valid adders occasionally would
look like a successful search.

Every candidate is scored by compiling it with upstream's compiler and running the netlist that
comes out. See [`MorphoEvaluator`](languages.md#morphospec-kt-morphoevaluator).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoSearch.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoSearch/)

**Used in:** [Searching for MorphoHDL Circuits](../morpho_search.md)

## MorphoSearchFLines.kt { #morphosearchflines-kt }

Drawing what a search did, as vector `FLine`s for [`afield.geometry.spatial.showPlaneGrid`](graphics.md#spatial-field-kt--showplanegrid).

Two figures, and between them they are the whole argument:

* [`morphoConvergenceFLines`](languages.md#morphosearchflines-kt--morphoconvergenceflines) — best-so-far error against compiler invocations, one line per
  driver. This is where the **control arm** lives: the random-search line and the evolution line
  are drawn on the same axes at the same budget, so "the search found it" is a statement about
  the gap between two curves rather than about one number.
* [`morphoParetoFLines`](languages.md#morphosearchflines-kt--morphoparetoflines) — gates against depth for every *correct* design found, with morpho's own
  hand-written designs marked. A search result that lands outside the human front is a result;
  one that lands on it is a different and much smaller result; and the picture says which.

Everything here is geometry. Nothing rasterises, so a figure scales, exports to SVG, and can be
redrawn every frame of a launched box while the search is still running.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoSearchFLines.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/morpho/MorphoSearchFLines/)

## MorphoSim.kt { #morphosim-kt }

What a compiled MorphoHDL circuit computes, and how deep it is: a bit-parallel logic simulator,
plus the per-cell arrival times morpho's own compiler already hands over.

[`MorphoSim`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphosim) evaluates a [`MorphoNetlist`](languages.md#morphonetlist-kt-morphonetlist) with 64 test vectors packed into the bits of a machine
word, which makes exhausting a small adder's whole input space cheap enough for a unit test.
Morpho's JavaScript has no logic simulator at all, so this side is Field's, written to the LUT
convention of the numpy evaluator in upstream's `tiny_morpho.py`. [`MorphoTiming`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphotiming) is the other way
round: a thin reading of morpho's own `updateTimes()`, whose deepest cell is the circuit's
critical path. [`MorphoEvaluator`](languages.md#morphospec-kt-morphoevaluator) reads both, the simulator for correctness and the arrival times
for depth.

## MorphoSpec.kt { #morphospec-kt }

What a MorphoHDL design is *supposed* to do, and how much it is allowed to cost — the half of a
search that morpho itself has no opinion about.

Everything in this file evaluates candidate designs by running them: [`MorphoRuntime`](languages.md#morphograal-kt-morphoruntime) compiles the
candidate's source with upstream's parser and upstream's compiler, [`MorphoSim`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphosim) runs the resulting
netlist, and [`MorphoTiming`](languages.md#morphosim-kt-morphotiming) — morpho's own `updateTimes()` — supplies the depth. Nothing here
models a circuit. A search whose fitness function was Field's idea of what a netlist would look
like would be searching Field's imagination, and the point of the bridge is that it does not have
to.

## NanoAssembler.kt { #nanoassembler-kt }

Turns Nano assembly source text into a bytecode `ByteArray`: one pass over the lines emitting
bytes, then a patch pass that fills in the labels the first pass left as placeholders.

`NanoVM.kt` has the machine and the opcode map; this is the text side of the same instruction
set. The listing below is the whole language: one directive, no macros, and operands that are
registers, integer literals or labels.

### Syntax

```diffstatic {data-lang=nano}
; line comment (rest of line)
label:            ; defines a label at the current address

; Data directive – place raw bytes into the program stream
.data 0x1A 0x2B 42 ...

; Instructions
nop
hlt
ret
inc r0
dec r1
not r2
neg r3
clr r0
out r1           ; print reg value
rng r2           ; fill with random byte

mov r0, r1       ; r0 = r1
add r0, r1       ; r0 += r1
sub r0, r1
mul r0, r1
and r0, r1
or  r0, r1
xor r0, r1
cmp r0, r1       ; flags = r0 <=> r1  (no reg change)
ldr r0, r1       ; r0 = the RAM byte at address r1  (load indirect)
str r0, r1       ; the RAM byte at address r0 = r1  (store indirect)
div r0, r1       ; r0 = r0 / r1  (integer; r1==0 → r0=0xFF)

ldi r0, 42       ; r0 = 42   (immediate, 0–255)
ldi r0, 0xFF
lda r0, 5        ; r0 = RAM[5]  (absolute load)
sta r0, 5        ; RAM[5] = r0  (absolute store)
addi r0, -3      ; r0 += -3     (signed immediate, -128..127)
ldrr r0, -2      ; r0 = RAM[PC + (-2)]  (PC-relative load)
strr r0, 4       ; RAM[PC + 4] = r0     (PC-relative store)
shl r0, 2        ; r0 <<= 2
shr r0, 1        ; r0 >>= 1

jmp  target      ; unconditional (relative, or label)
jz   target
jnz  target
jgt  target
jlt  target
jge  target
jle  target
jc   target
jnc  target
call target      ; relative call
jmpa target      ; absolute jump (0–255)
calla target     ; absolute call
```

Labels can appear on their own line (`start:`) or before a mnemonic on the same line
(`start: ldi r0, 0`).  A label used by a relative branch resolves to the
**signed 8-bit offset from the byte following the branch** (PC+2 for the two-byte forms like
`jmp`), and an offset that will not fit in −128..+127 is an error on that line. `jmpa` and
`calla` take the absolute address instead, so there the error is an address past 255.

### Results and errors

Every bad register, number, mnemonic, duplicate label and out-of-range branch goes into a list
that assembly keeps filling, so one run reports all of them with the line each came from rather
than stopping at the first. `assemble` hands back `AssemblyResult`, which is either the bytes
or that list. `assembleWithSourceMap` hands back the same bytes plus a program-counter-to-line
array, which is what `NanoInterface.kt` and `NanoVisualization.kt` use to mark the source line a
running program is on. The throwing wrapper a live-coding box calls is the top-level
`nanoAssemble` in `NanoInterface.kt`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/nano/NanoAssembler.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/nano/NanoAssembler/)
