## NanoComputeShader.kt { #nanocomputeshader-kt }

The host side of `nano_compute.glsl`, the GLSL compute port of the Nano VM: the buffer layout a caller has to honour,
the mapping struct, and the packing helpers for getting bytes in and out.

The shader runs one independent Nano VM instance per GPU invocation, decoding the same opcode map `NanoVM.kt`
documents. Three of its four storage buffers hold bytes and are cut into non-overlapping per-instance slices; the
fourth, at binding 0, holds one `NanoMapping` per dispatch id and says where that instance's three slices begin.
**Nothing in the tree dispatches it.** `SOURCE` reads the GLSL off the classpath and the helpers below build the
buffers, so what is missing is the Vulkan plumbing: pipeline, descriptor sets, submit and readback.

### Buffer bindings
| binding | layout           | access | description                    |
|---------|------------------|--------|--------------------------------|
| 0       | `NanoMapping[]`  | r-only | dispatch-id → slice offsets    |
| 1       | `uint[]` (bytes) | r/w    | RAM: persistent working memory |
| 2       | `uint[]` (bytes) | r-only | code: assembled Nano programs  |
| 3       | `uint[]` (bytes) | r/w    | OUT stream: results of OUT rX  |

#### Byte-packing

All three byte buffers pack 4 bytes per `uint`: the byte at logical offset B lives in word `B >> 2` at bit-shift `(B
& 3) << 3`. A host has to honour that when uploading code and RAM and when reading OUT results back, which is what
`packBytes`, `packPrograms` and `unpackBytes` are for.

### Push constants (20 bytes, std430)
| field           | type   | description                                    |
|-----------------|--------|------------------------------------------------|
| numInstances    | uint32 | total instances (over-dispatch guard)          |
| defaultMaxSteps | uint32 | step limit when mapping.maxSteps == 0          |
| ramSize         | uint32 | RAM bytes per instance; **must be power-of-2** |
| codeSize        | uint32 | code bytes per instance (≤ 256)                |

### Mapping buffer layout (NanoMapping struct, 20 bytes each)
| field          | type   | description                                    |
|----------------|--------|------------------------------------------------|
| ramBase        | uint32 | byte offset into RAM buffer for this instance  |
| codeBase       | uint32 | byte offset into code buffer for this instance |
| outputBase     | uint32 | byte offset into OUT buffer for this instance  |
| maxSteps       | uint32 | per-instance step cap (0 → use push-constant)  |
| outputCapacity | uint32 | maximum OUT bytes; overflow halts this VM      |

### Minimal dispatch example (pseudocode)

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val N         = 1024               // number of Nano instances
val ramSize   = 32                 // bytes per VM
val codeSize  = 64                 // bytes per program
val outSize   = 64                 // max OUT bytes per VM

val mappings  = NanoComputeShader.buildMappings(N, ramSize, codeSize, outSize)
// upload mappings, ramBytes (N*ramSize), codeBytes (N*codeSize), outBytes (N*outSize)
// bind as buffers 0..3
// dispatch ceil(N / 64) groups of 64
```

## NanoDisassembler.kt { #nanodisassembler-kt }

Reads a Nano bytecode `ByteArray` back as assembly text, one `DisasmLine` per instruction.

It walks the program twice. The first walk collects every branch target, so that the second can
put a name on each one and a branch reads as a label rather than as a raw offset. The name is
the target address in hex, so `L00` and `L0A`, and it arrives as its own `DisasmLine` with an
empty `bytes` list, which is how `NanoVisualization.kt` tells a label apart from an instruction
when it is deciding which line to highlight.

`DisasmLine.toString` is the printable form:

    addr:  hex  hex   mnemonic  operands    ; optional annotation

The annotation is the part the bytes do not say: the signed offset behind a relative branch, and
the absolute address behind `jmpa` or `calla`. A byte that decodes to no instruction prints as
`???` with its hex value, which is the five of the 256 that `NanoVM.kt` lists as executing
nothing: `0x03`, and `0xFC`–`0xFF` past `DIV`'s last register pair.

## NanoInterface.kt { #nanointerface-kt }

Field4 language adapter for the Nano 8-bit assembly language.

Nano is a compact virtual machine: 4 registers (r0–r3), 32 bytes of RAM with address
wrap, a small call stack, and an instruction set sized for emergence and artificial-life
grid experiments. [`NanoExecution`](languages.md#nanointerface-kt-nanoexecution) is the [`BoxExecution`](workspace.md#execution-kt-boxexecution) implementation; setting a parent
box's `isNanoRoot` to `true` turns its children into Nano assembly boxes.

[`installNano`](languages.md#nanointerface-kt--installnano) registers the runtime with Field's language dispatch; [`installNanoPlugin`](languages.md#nanointerface-kt--installnanoplugin)
starts the topology watcher that activates it when the box tree changes. [`nanoAssemble`](languages.md#nanointerface-kt--nanoassemble)
and [`Box.nanoDisassemble`](languages.md#nanointerface-kt--nanodisassemble) are available to neighbouring Kotlin boxes that need to inspect
or construct the VM's byte representation directly.

## NanoVM.kt { #nanovm-kt }

Nano is a minimal 8-bit virtual machine designed for emergence and artificial-life simulations:
four registers, 32 bytes of RAM, and all but five of the 256 possible opcode bytes decoding to an
instruction.

The whole machine is:

 - `r0`–`r3`, 8-bit unsigned, so 0–255
 - 32 bytes of RAM, addressed modulo 32, so no address is out of range
 - flags `Z` (zero), `C` (carry), `S` (sign) and `O` (overflow)
 - a call stack eight deep, for `CALL` and `RET`
 - unsigned-byte arithmetic throughout, wrapping mod 256

Instructions are fetched from the program byte array passed to `NanoVM.run`, and `ram` is
separate data. `NanoVM.load` also mirrors the program's first 32 bytes into RAM, which is what
lets a program read its own text. `NanoInterface`'s launch mode calls `NanoVM.resetRegisters`
instead, leaving RAM alone so it carries state from one per-tick run to the next.

### Opcode map

[`Opcode`](languages.md#nanovm-kt-opcode) is the constant table, and `Opcode.twoReg` and `Opcode.oneReg` are the encoders.

| form | encoding | instructions | opcodes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| no operand | one byte | `NOP`, `HLT`, `RET` | `0x00`–`0x02` |
| one register | `base + reg`, 4 per op | `INC`, `DEC`, `NOT`, `NEG`, `CLR`, `OUT`, `RNG` | `0x04`–`0x1F` |
| two registers | `base + (dst shl 2) + src`, 16 per op | `MOV`, `ADD`, `SUB`, `MUL`, `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`, `CMP`, `LDR`, `STR` | `0x20`–`0xBF` |
| register and immediate or address | two bytes, 4 per op | `LDI`, `LDA`, `STA`, `ADDI`, `LDRR`, `STRR`, `SHL`, `SHR` | `0xC0`–`0xDF` |
| relative branch | two bytes, signed offset | `JMP`, `JZ`, `JNZ`, `JGT`, `JLT`, `JGE`, `JLE`, `JC`, `JNC`, `CALL` | `0xE0`–`0xE9` |
| absolute branch | two bytes, absolute address | `JMPA`, `CALLA` | `0xEA`–`0xEB` |
| two registers | `base + (dst shl 2) + src` | `DIV` | `0xEC`–`0xFB` |

Five bytes decode to nothing — `0x03`, and `0xFC`–`0xFF` past `DIV`'s last `(dst, src)` pair.
Each reports an unknown opcode and halts. That path matters here more than it would in a VM with
a fixed program: artificial-life work mutates programs, and `NanoAssembler`'s raw-byte directive
puts an arbitrary byte in front of the decoder too, so every one of the 256 has to either execute
or report. The GPU port in `nano_compute.glsl` decodes the same map.

### A program

```diffstatic {data-lang=nano}
; comment
start:
    ldi r0, 10     ; r0 = 10
    ldi r1, 0      ; r1 = 0
loop:
    add r1, r0     ; r1 += r0
    dec r0         ; r0--  (sets Z when r0 reaches 0)
    jnz loop       ; jump back if not zero
    out r1         ; print r1
    hlt
```

`NanoAssembler.kt` has the rest of the syntax, including the directive that places raw bytes in
the program stream and the fact that a label resolves to an offset for a relative branch and to
an address for `JMPA` and `CALLA`.

## NanoVisualization.kt { #nanovisualization-kt }

Runs a Nano program and hands back its final machine state, either as data or as a self-contained
HTML panel for a box's output area.

Nothing in the repository calls these; they exist for a Kotlin box sitting next to a Nano box, so
a document can show a register file and 32 bytes of RAM without reaching into [`NanoVM`](languages.md#nanovm-kt-nanovm) itself.
`nanoRunReportHtml` is the one-liner and `nanoRunReport` is the same run with the state left as a
[`NanoRunReport`](languages.md#nanovisualization-kt-nanorunreport) to read or render differently.

The two kinds of failure a Nano program can have come back by different routes. Source that will
not assemble throws `NanoAssemblyException` from either entry point, because there is no machine
state to report. A program that assembles and then faults at run time fills `runtimeError` and
returns everything else, because the registers and RAM at the point of the fault are what a
reader wants; `nanoRunReportHtml` turns that into a thrown `IllegalStateException` by default,
and `throwOnRuntimeError = false` gets the panel with the error drawn into it instead. A program
that never halts is neither: `maxSteps` bounds the run and `halted` comes back false.

`RNG` draws from `Random` unless `rngSeed` is given, so a program using it is reproducible only
when seeded.

The rendered panel distinguishes three things about a RAM cell, and only two of them survive this
route. A cell whose value differs from the program byte loaded there is drawn as mutated, and the
cell under the program counter is drawn as current. `changedRegisters` and `changedRam` draw what
the most recent step touched, and only a single-step caller fills them, so a panel from
`nanoRunReport` shows accumulated mutation and never per-step change.

## NumpyShared.kt { #numpyshared-kt }

Shared memory between Python boxes and Kotlin boxes: images and line sets that numpy writes in
place and Kotlin reads without copying through a serializer.

[`NumpyShared`](languages.md#numpyshared-kt-numpyshared) hands out named [`SharedImage`](languages.md#numpyshared-kt-sharedimage) and [`SharedLines`](languages.md#numpyshared-kt-sharedlines) buffers; the `fieldcv` package in
`python/` is the Python side. `NumpySharedTest` covers the publish/consume handoff.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/python/NumpyShared.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/python/NumpyShared/)

### SharedImage { #numpyshared-kt-sharedimage }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">SharedImage</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">height</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">width</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/python/NumpyShared/#L106)

## PythonErrors.kt { #pythonerrors-kt }

Error locations for Python boxes: the cell line that raised, read from the exception's traceback.

[`PythonErrors`](languages.md#pythonerrors-kt-pythonerrors) holds the Python helper spliced into the interpreter and the Kotlin arithmetic that
maps its answer onto a box line. `PythonErrorsTest` runs the helper under a plain `python3`.

## PythonInterface.kt { #pythoninterface-kt }

Python as a Field main language: a box whose source is Python, executed **in this process** by
CPython through JEP.

There is no subprocess and no socket, so a Python box and a Kotlin box exchange objects rather
than text; and there is exactly **one interpreter and one namespace per Field process**, so two
Python boxes share globals whether or not you wanted them to. That is a deliberate trade — it is
what makes a cell in one box see a `DataFrame` another box built — and it is the first thing to
know before debugging "why does this variable already exist".

Read it in four layers:

 - **Configuration.** JEP needs a real CPython to bind against, chosen once and persisted:
   [`PythonSettingsRequest`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythonsettingsrequest), [`PythonSettingsStatus`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythonsettingsstatus) and [`PythonInstallResult`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythoninstallresult) are that
   negotiation, and `restartRequired` means it: a new interpreter binding cannot be swapped
   into a live JVM. [`makeInterpreter`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt--makeinterpreter) runs early and returns silently when nothing is
   configured, which is why a checkout with no Python simply has no Python boxes rather than a
   broken startup.
 - **[`PythonExecution`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt-pythonexecution)**, the `BoxExecution`. Beyond the usual output proxying it carries the
   cooperative event loop: an `asyncio` loop implemented in Python that yields to Field's runloop
   instead of blocking it, so `await` inside a box does not stop the editor.
 - **Output.** Everything a box prints funnels through one formatter, and three cases are
   special: a `\r` becomes a Field progress bar (which is how `tqdm` renders as a real one),
   an object exposing `HTML`/`Image`/`Markdown`/`Math`/`JSON` renders as itself, and a library
   that tries to open a browser page — plotly's `fig.show()`, bokeh, folium — is intercepted and
   the HTML delivered into the box as an iframe `srcdoc`. Nothing here opens a browser.
 - **Registration.** [`installPython`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt--installpython) and [`pythonTopologyNeedsUpdating`](languages.md#pythoninterface-kt--pythontopologyneedsupdating) are the same two-call
   shape every main language uses; see `dev_docs/small_language_anatomy.md`.

A large part of this file is Python source held in Kotlin string literals — the event loop, the
display types, the output shims. It is code that has to run *inside* the interpreter, so it lives
here rather than in a `.py` on disk, where a fresh checkout could be missing it.

[Python in Field](../python.md) is the prose.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/python/PythonInterface.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/python/PythonInterface/)

## PythonLineNotes.kt { #pythonlinenotes-kt }

Line notes for Python boxes: a rewriter that records what each top-level statement of a cell
evaluated to, for display beside the code.

[`PythonLineNotes`](languages.md#pythonlinenotes-kt-pythonlinenotes) carries the rewriter as Python source and the environment switch that disables
it. `PythonLineNotesTest` runs that source under a plain `python3`.

## RectSL.kt { #rectsl-kt }

RectSL — Field's rectangle scene language, and the largest single file in the tree.

A RectSL program is a *finite animated scene made of rectangles*, written as a small stack
language inside a Kotlin triple-quoted string whose first line is `#rectsl`. It is not a
simulation and not a renderer: the language decides where rectangles are over a fixed duration
and what material metadata each one carries, and StackSL (`afield.lang.stacksl`) decides how a
material shades. That division is the reason both are small.

### The pipeline, in reading order

Four types, and every entry point in this file is a step between two of them:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
String  --tokenize-->  List<Token>  --eval-->  SceneProgram  --sample(t)-->  SampledScene  --lower-->  RectMesh
```

 - [`RectLangTokenizer`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectlangtokenizer) is the whole of the syntax. There is no parser: the language is
   postfix, so tokenizing *is* parsing.
 - [`RectLangVm`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectlangvm) is the evaluator, and where the vocabulary lives. Words spelled `->something`
   are mutators that write through to the active rect, group or scene; everything else
   transforms stack values. The arrow is part of the word.
 - [`SceneProgram`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sceneprogram) is the compiled result and the value worth understanding first. It is
   **time-independent** — a wall, a duration, an fps and a list of nodes whose properties are
   [`Track`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-track)s rather than numbers — which is what makes a scene something you can ask questions
   of rather than only play. `sample(t)` walks it and returns a [`SampledScene`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sampledscene), a flat
   z-ordered list of [`SampledRect`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sampledrect)s with no tracks left in it.
 - [`lowerSampledScene`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--lowersampledscene) turns that into a [`RectMesh`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectmesh): four [`RectVertex`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectvertex)es and six indices per
   rect, with colour, material index and per-object shader data interleaved, ready for a
   Vulkan buffer.

[`RectAnimationOracle`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-rectanimationoracle) is the one object that names all five steps, and
[`compileRectSL`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--compilerectsl) is the same compile with host-built curves bound in by name — the
`afield.math.functions.Functions` half of the bridge, so a program can lay out an array from a curve the
host fitted or evolved.

### Why a property is a track and not a number

Half this file is [`Track`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-track) and its implementations, because a property being a function of time
rather than a number is what the rest of the package is built on. A track is symbolic and
composable — [`TcbTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-tcbtrack) for Kochanek–Bartels keys, [`EasedScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-easedscalartrack), [`TimeWarpTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-timewarptrack),
[`GateTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-gatetrack) for life windows, [`HeadingTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-headingtrack) for face-travel, plus unary/binary/ternary
combinators — so a scene can be *differentiated*, *fitted* (`RectSLFit.kt`), *measured*
(`RectSLCoverage.kt` computes exact pixel coverage in closed form) and *translated* to GLSL
(`RectSLGlsl.kt`) rather than only evaluated frame by frame.

### Where the rest of the package sits

`RectSLPattern.kt` / `RectSLPatternOps.kt` make a Tidal pattern the scene's structure — a
pattern is a track and an event is a live window. `RectSLSoftRaster.kt` is the differentiable
rasterizer, `RectSLFn.kt` lowers scenes into the `Functions` algebra, `RectSLSdfLook.kt` and
`RectSLGlsl.kt` are the two GPU paths, `RectSLSimplify.kt` shrinks a program, and
`RectSLEditorExtension.kt` is the three lines that register the browser-side editor mode.

[RectSL cheatsheet](../rectsl_cheatsheet.md) is the word-by-word reference with worked pictures;
[RectSL examples](../rectsl_examples.md) is the gallery.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSL.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSL/)

**Used in:** [RectSL Inverse Animation](../rectsl_inverse_animation.md), [RectSL examples](../rectsl_examples.md), [RectSL cheatsheet](../rectsl_cheatsheet.md)

A hard visibility window — 1.0 while `lo <= t < hi`, else 0.0. Multiplied into an object's alpha, it makes the object pop into and out of existence at fixed times (bullet spawn/despawn). `lo`/`hi` default to ±infinity for one-sided gates.

Rotation derived from a pair of position tracks: the heading (direction of travel) of the point (x(t), y(t)). Because RectSL tracks are pure closed-form functions of time, the velocity is recovered by central finite difference — no simulation state — so a rect can auto-orient to its own trajectory. `offset` corrects for how the rect's art is drawn (0 = local +x points along travel).

### FrameSemanticMetrics { #rectsl-kt-framesemanticmetrics }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">FrameSemanticMetrics</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">time</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">visibleObjectCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">totalVisibleAreaSquareMeters</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">averageVelocity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2d</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">averageSpeedMetersPerSecond</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">averageAngularVelocityRadiansPerSecond</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">totalOpacityWeightedArea</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSL/#L1478)

What one sampled frame shows. A rectangle counts as *visible* when it is not transparent and meets the wall, and the areas count only the part of it inside the wall (its bounding box's share, for a rotated one) — so a rectangle waiting below the wall to rise into it is not counted. Until 2026-09-27 every opaque rectangle counted wherever it was, which made a scene whose rectangles had all left the wall look fully occupied, and [`AnimationWarning.MostlyBlank`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--animationwarning--mostlyblank) never fire for it.

## RectSLCoverage.kt { #rectslcoverage-kt }

The **exact** coverage a soft raster is approximating, and the measurement of how far off it is.

### Why the reference has to be exact

A soft rasterizer is only useful if you know what it is wrong about. The claim a differentiable
renderer makes is "coverage is a smooth function of the parameters"; the claim it must not make is
"coverage is *correct*". Between those two sits a bias, and a bias you have not measured is a bias
your fit has silently absorbed into its answer.

So this file computes the thing there is no argument about: the **area** of a pixel covered by the
scene, in closed form. A rect is a convex quadrilateral and a pixel is a convex box, so a single
rect's coverage is a convex-convex clip ([`clipConvexToBox`](languages.md#rectslcoverage-kt--clipconvextobox), Sutherland–Hodgman) followed by the
shoelace formula ([`polygonArea`](languages.md#rectslcoverage-kt--polygonarea)) — exact in the arithmetic, with no sampling anywhere. A *union* of
rects is not convex, so that case goes to JTS, an outside implementation of the same quantity,
which makes it a check on this file rather than a restatement of it.
`RectSLSoftRasterTest` cross-checks the two on the single-rect case where both apply.

### The three biases, named

The measurement in [`measureCoverageBias`](languages.md#rectslcoverage-kt--measurecoveragebias) is designed around the fact that there are three
*different* reasons soft coverage departs from area coverage, and lumping them together produces a
number that means nothing:

1. **Obliquity.** Every kernel in [`CoverageKernel`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-coveragekernel) is a function of a single signed distance, so it
   is implicitly assuming the edge is axis-aligned. For an axis-aligned edge the exact area of a
   unit pixel on one side of it *is* `clamp(0.5 - d)`, so [`CoverageKernel`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-coveragekernel)'s `LINEAR` at `beta` =
   one pixel has **zero** obliquity bias there, which is itself a check: if that case does not come
   out at machine precision, either the kernel or the exact reference is wrong. As the edge rotates
   the true coverage curve becomes piecewise quadratic and the ramp cannot follow it.
2. **Feature scale.** A rect thinner than the band never lets coverage saturate. As
   width/`beta` → 0 the error tends to the whole of the feature's coverage, which is the regime
   where a soft raster is not an approximation of the picture at all.
3. **Union seams.** `min` of two signed distances is the union's distance *outside* the union and
   an under-estimate *inside* it, so where two rects abut the field reads about zero and coverage
   collapses towards 0.5 across a region that is entirely covered. This one is a property of the
   SDF, not of the kernel, and it is the reason [`CoverageComposite`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-coveragecomposite) has two members.

Each is reported separately, over a population that is counted so that an empty population cannot
read as a pass: see [`CoverageBiasRow.partialPixels`](languages.md#rectslcoverage-kt--coveragebiasrow--partialpixels) and [`CoverageBiasRow.edgePixels`](languages.md#rectslcoverage-kt--coveragebiasrow--edgepixels).

### Scope of the reference

Area coverage is defined for **opaque** geometry. A rect at alpha 0.4 has no area interpretation —
the exact answer to "what fraction of this pixel is covered" is still 1 if the rect fills it — so
[`exactRaster`](languages.md#rectslcoverage-kt--exactraster) treats every visible rect as opaque and [`measureCoverageBias`](languages.md#rectslcoverage-kt--measurecoveragebias) throws on a scene
whose rects are translucent, instead of returning a number that compares two different quantities.

## RectSLEditorExtension.kt { #rectsleditorextension-kt }

Serves `rectsl.js`, the browser-side RectSL editor support, to the page and to the test that
checks it.

RectSL runs in Kotlin, in `RectSL.kt`; a RectSL program is a triple-quoted string beginning
`#rectsl` inside an ordinary Kotlin box. So there is no execution path to hook, and this file is
the whole of the language's presence in the editor. `rectsl.js` lives in
`src/commonMain/resources`, reaches the browser as the AMD module `bithero/rectsl` (one of the
modules `bootstrapMonaco.js` requires by name while the editor starts), and is read back verbatim
here, so the smoke test `rectsl.editor-extension.workout` runs the same bytes the editor does. A
browser-side language that can only be tested in a browser does not stay correct.

Once installed, the extension brings syntax highlighting, flow decorations, lexical diagnostics,
a context badge and completions to a `#rectsl` region. Colouring is decoration-based rather than a
Monarch grammar, so there is no grammar here that can fail to compile and take Monaco's startup
down with it.

`rectsl.js` installs itself either way it is loaded: as an AMD module when a Monaco loader
is present, and immediately when it is evaluated bare, which is the path `html()` uses. The two
differ in one respect. The AMD path also registers a standalone `rectsl` Monaco language, so that
a loose `.rectsl` file opened in the editor gets `#` comment toggling and bracket handling; it
carries no tokenizer of its own, because the decoration highlighter already treats a whole
`rectsl` model as one region.

## RectSLFit.kt { #rectslfit-kt }

Inverse animation: say where a rect should be and when, and solve for the numbers.

This is what the differentiable backend is *for*. A RectSL program is normally read forwards —
you write the tracks and the sampler tells you where the rects went. Once a track lowers to an
`Fn` the arrow turns round: [`FreeParamTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-freeparamtrack) marks the numbers you are willing to have chosen for
you, [`TrackFitTarget`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt-trackfittarget) says what the track should read at particular instants, and the exact
gradient of the lowered graph walks the parameters to the answer.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
# a bar whose height is unknown
1.0 free-param height
```
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val fit = track.fitParameters(listOf(TrackFitTarget(0.5, 3.0), TrackFitTarget(1.5, 0.0)))
fit.initialResidual   // where the seed was
fit.finalResidual     // where the fit ended
fit.fitted            // the same track, with the parameters substituted
```

### Why this is not simply `fitGradient`

`fitGradient` is the library's fitter and it does the right thing for a whole graph: it moves
**every** numeric leaf. A lowered track's leaves are mostly not parameters at all — they are the
key times, the clamp bounds, the `0.5` in an easing, the `-1.0` that mirrors a reversed clock.
Letting a descent move those would not fit a track, it would dismantle one. So the loss and the
Adam update here are the same shape as `fitGradient`'s, over a **mask**: only the θ slots that
[`freeParameterSlots`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt--freeparameterslots) identified as named parameters ever move — *slots*, plural, because a
lowering may use one sub-`Fn` more than once and each occurrence gets its own θ index. A heading
reads each of its position tracks twelve times. The slots of one name are one variable here:
gradients summed, one Adam moment, one step written to all of them.

Everything under the mask is borrowed rather than reimplemented. The gradient is
[`Functions.Fn.gradientAt`](function.md#autodiff-fn-kt--gradientat) — one forward interpretation and one backward sweep through the same
`FnFormulas` table `Fn.eval` is pinned against — and θ is read and written by
`extractParameters` / `applyParameters`, so index *i* means the same leaf here as it does there.

A track that does not lower cannot be fitted, and says so with the lowering's own reason rather
than a generic failure. A track that lowers but has no free parameters is refused too: descending
on an empty mask would report "converged" without having moved, which is the failure mode
`FnNonDifferentiable` exists to prevent.

## RectSLFitFigure.kt { #rectslfitfigure-kt }

A fit, as a picture, with its counterfactual beside it.

The figure stacks three bands: where the rect was asked to be, where the seed parameters put it,
and where the solved parameters put it. The miss and its correction are visible in one image.

It is a CPU raster. The GPU path needs a device, a window and a render target; this runs in a unit
test and inside a Field box. Every rectangle on the canvas is one [`SampledRect`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sampledrect), sampled from the
fitted tracks at the drawn times, so a failed fit shows in the third band.

RectSL has no text primitive (its axis labels are grids of rects), so the band labels use the 3×5
dot-matrix font the plotting words use for tick numerals.

## RectSLFn.kt { #rectslfn-kt }

RectSL tracks as differentiable `Fn` graphs — the third backend.

### Why there is a third backend at all

The track IR is symbolic rather than a closure, because a closure cannot be printed, compared,
rewritten, or emitted as GLSL. [`TrackOp1`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop1), [`TrackOp2`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop2), [`TrackOp3`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop3) and [`TimeWarpKind`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-timewarpkind)
each carry an `eval:` and a `glsl:`; this file is the third column, `fn:`, and it is the one that
changes what RectSL can *do* rather than where it can run.

[`afield.math.functions.Functions.Fn`](math.md#functions-kt--functions--fn) is Field's own expression type, and `autodiff_fn.kt` differentiates
an `Fn` graph exactly with respect to its numeric leaves. So a track that lowers to an `Fn` is a
track you can take the derivative of, and therefore a track you can **solve**: declare where a
rect should be at some instant and let a gradient find the numbers that put it there. That is
[`Track.fitParameters`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt--fitparameters), and it is the point of this file.

### The two identities that make it possible

`Fn` was not designed as a general expression language, and two gaps look fatal and are not.

**There is no "apply a unary function to another `Fn`'s value" op.** The differentiable value
transforms are `flip`, `abs`, `exp`, `log`, `pow`, `clamp`, `scaleY`, `offsetY` and pointwise
arithmetic — no `sin`. `Functions.sin` is an *oscillator* over the sample position,
`offset + amplitude·sin(2π·frequency·x + phase)`, which is not a composition. But its `phase`
child is evaluated **at x**, so

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
sin(frequency = 0, phase = u, amplitude = 1, offset = 0)   ==   sin(u(x))
```

exactly (`0 + 1·sin(2π·0·x + u)` collapses with no rounding). That single identity gives the
whole trigonometric family, which is most of the Penner easings.

**There is no piecewise-in-x op, and every keyframed track is piecewise.** A clamped-ramp sum
fixes it. For keys `(tᵢ, vᵢ)` and any segment shape `Sᵢ` with `Sᵢ(0) = vᵢ` and `Sᵢ(1) = vᵢ₊₁`,

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
v(t)  =  v₀ + Σᵢ [ Sᵢ(clamp01((t - tᵢ) / (tᵢ₊₁ - tᵢ))) - vᵢ ]
```

is *identically* the clamped piecewise interpolant: for t inside span j every earlier term is
`vᵢ₊₁ - vᵢ` and every later one is 0, so the sum telescopes to `vⱼ + (vⱼ₊₁ - vⱼ)·Sⱼ(u)`. Before
the first key everything is 0 and after the last everything is 1, which is exactly the sampler's
clamping. It needs only clamp / divide / multiply / add, all differentiable, and it is exact to
a few ulps rather than approximate. [`LinearScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-linearscalartrack), [`EasedScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-easedscalartrack) and [`TcbTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-tcbtrack)
(whose tangents [`TcbTrack.hermiteSegments`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--tcbtrack--hermitesegments) has already resolved) all lower through it.

### Refusals are in the type

A wrong derivative is worse than no derivative, so the lowering never guesses. Every op declares
either a lowering or a refusal *with a reason* — [`RectSLFnLowering`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt-rectslfnlowering) — and [`Track.toFn`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt--tofn) propagates
the first refusal it meets. This is the same discipline `FnNonDifferentiable` already applies
inside the stdlib, and for the same reason: the gap has to be readable, or it grows in silence.

What is refused:

- `TrackOp2.MOD`. Kotlin's `%` on doubles is the *exact* remainder, and `a - b·trunc(a/b)` in
  double arithmetic is a different function once the quotient outgrows 53 bits: `1e17 % 3` is
  `1.0` and the reconstruction says `0.0`. Silently, and as a zero, which is indistinguishable
  from the guard having fired. A constant pair still folds.
- The pattern tracks ([`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack) and friends) — an interpreter over a mini-notation tree, not an
  expression of fixed shape. `PatPattern` is a `(PatArc) -> List<PatEvent>` lambda: there is
  nothing to inspect and no closed form to find, which is the same reason `FnNonDifferentiable`
  files `pat` itself, and makes this the one refusal here that cannot be closed. It has a name,
  [`RECTSL_PATTERN_REFUSAL`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt--rectsl-pattern-refusal), and a predicate that decides it from the track rather than from the
  sentence: [`dependsOnPatternTrack`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt--dependsonpatterntrack). It costs far less than four rhythm scenes in the gallery
  would suggest — 27 of 5020 tracks — because `pat` used as *scene structure* is unrolled at
  compile time into one gated rect per event, so no interpreter
  survives into the sampled IR, and `musicality-variation` lowers all 1096 of its tracks despite
  spending six `pat` verbs. What survives is a pattern still being asked a value of at sample
  time: a signal word read as a channel — `sine`, `cosine`, `saw`, `isaw`, `tri`, `square`,
  `perlin`, `rand` all push a `VSig`, and `VSig.asTrack` is a [`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack) — or one of the two
  gates the pattern layer installs on a rect's alpha, `->every` on the cycle count and
  `->degrade` on a per-event coin flip. Those are the same tracks the GLSL/SDF emitter has to
  bake rather than lower: the one place both backends meet the same wall.
- Degenerate keyed tracks: no keys at all (nothing to sample), or two keys sharing a time (a step
  between two named values, which the clamped-ramp identity cannot express).

Everything else lowers exactly, hard edges included. `Fn` has a first-class differentiable
`floor`, from which `ceil` is `-floor(-x)` and `fract` is `x - floor(x)`, both exact in IEEE, and
the `loop` and `pingpong` time warps follow for any window. `clamp01(floor(x) + 1)` is an *exact*
step — 1 at and above 0, 0 below, at every double including `-0.0` — which gives
[`HoldScalarTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-holdscalartrack) as `v₀ + Σ (vᵢ - vᵢ₋₁)·[t ≥ tᵢ]` and [`GateTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-gatetrack) straddling an edge as
`[t ≥ lo]·(1 - [t ≥ hi])`, the sampler's half-open boundary included. Zero-almost-everywhere is
the *truth* about a staircase rather than an approximation of one, so [`Track.fitParameters`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt--fitparameters)
refuses a parameter reachable only through a step instead of descending a gradient that cannot
move.

`withExactEndpoints` below covers the expo and elastic easings, whose closed forms do not reach
their own endpoints. `lowerHeading` covers [`HeadingTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-headingtrack) through `atan2`, and records the one
signed-zero corner where it parts
company with the sampler. `fnGuardedQuotient` guards the *divisor* of a near-zero division, as
`b·live + (1 - live)`, so nothing ever divides by a near-zero and no infinity is created to
mask; the sign of the suppressed zero is repaired by adding `fnZeroSelector`'s `-0.0`/`+0.0`,
since `x + -0.0` is the true additive identity on doubles and `x + +0.0` is not.

`dev_docs/stdlib_behaviour_changes.md` carries the dates on which each of those stopped being a
refusal, and what it means for a scene written before then.

### How the fidelity is checked

`RectSLFnBackendTest` is the reason to believe any of this. It reads
`src/jvmTest/resources/rectsl/track_characterization.txt` — every sampled rect of the gallery's
programs at 41 times, to full double precision — as data, and recomputes each rect's channels
through Fn-lowered tracks, so the oracle shares no code path with the thing under test. It
reports the worst disagreement, and it reports coverage, how much of the corpus lowered at all,
because a differential test that refused everything would otherwise read as a pass.

The corpus is not uniform in what it proves, and its rows differ in what they rule out. The
rows for the programs that predate this backend were dumped from code that knew nothing about
it, so a disagreement on one of those can only be this file's. The rows for the four
`musicality-*` programs were produced by the current [`SceneProgram.sample`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--sceneprogram--sample): still a real
differential, since the symbolic IR shares no code path with the sampler, but not independent of
a sampler bug introduced since. Nothing should be re-derived from those four as if it were.

## RectSLGlsl.kt { #rectslglsl-kt }

RectSL scenes as GLSL signed distance fields.

### Why this is a small file

RectSL looks like a big language to port, and almost none of it needs
porting. The stack VM is a *build-time* machine: `array`, `grid`, `radial`,
every selection word, `each`/`filter`, the chart and plotting layers, the
`{{ }}` Kotlin escapes — all of it runs once and is gone, leaving a
[`SceneProgram`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-sceneprogram): a flat list of nodes whose channels are [`Track`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-track)s. Only that
residue has to reach the GPU, and it is eleven track shapes and a 2D
transform.

### What the SDF is, and is not

This emits shape, not picture. A RectSL scene is painter's-algorithm 2D —
z-sorted rects composited with per-rect alpha, fill, and material. An SDF is
a set, and `min` is union, which has no notion of layering. So the emitted
`float` field answers "how far is this point from the nearest visible
rectangle" and drops fill, material, and layer order. What that
buys is everything a distance field is good at and a rasterized quad is not:
outlines and glows at any width, `smin` blending *between* rectangles,
boolean ops, per-pixel normals, and sub-frame motion blur — because time is a
uniform and every track is closed-form, so a fragment can sample the scene at
as many instants as it likes.

Visibility is not dropped. A rect whose alpha has been gated to zero by
`->appear` / `->vanish` / `->live` must not contribute a silhouette, so each
rect's alpha track is evaluated and tested before its distance is unioned in.

None of that list is aspirational, and it is more useful to say where the
evidence is than to restate the claim. [`RectSLSdfLook`](languages.md#rectslsdflook-kt-rectslsdflook) is that vocabulary as
data with one preset per capability, [`RectSLSdfShader`](languages.md#rectslsdflook-kt-rectslsdfshader) assembles a whole
fragment shader from it, and `RectSLGalleryHarness.renderSdf` renders each
preset — plus a side-by-side against the raster path — into
`public/docs/assets/rectsl/rectsl-sdf-*.png`. Two of them need the emitter's
cooperation rather than the look layer's, because they change the *set*: see
[`RectSLSdfOptions`](languages.md#rectslglsl-kt-rectslsdfoptions). To get it on screen and moving, replay
`dev_docs/agents/transcripts/rectsl_sdf_live.yaml`.

### Fidelity

Tracks are emitted symbolically, never sampled into tables: keyed tracks
become branch chains, TCB tracks become cubic Hermite spans with their
tangents precomputed on the CPU ([`TcbTrack.hermiteSegments`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--tcbtrack--hermitesegments)), and the scalar
ops carry their own GLSL ([`TrackOp1`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop1), [`TrackOp2`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-trackop2), [`TimeWarpKind`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-timewarpkind)). The
guards are reproduced rather than approximated — RectSL's divide-by-zero
returns 0, and its `mod` truncates where GLSL's floors.

The one unavoidable difference is precision: the CPU samples in `double` and
a shader runs in `float`. Expect agreement to about 1e-6 of a wall unit, not
to the ulp. `RectSLGalleryHarness.measureSdfAgreement` reads the *compiled
shader's* own answers back out of a framebuffer and compares them against
[`SceneProgram.sample`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--sceneprogram--sample) across eleven programs, and the worst disagreement is
2.5e-06 wall units.

What *is* approximated is now two tracks, not three. `->degrade`'s 64-bit
integer hash reads like something a shader cannot do and is not: it lowers
**exactly**, in `uvec2` lanes, with the threshold comparison done in integers so
no float enters the decision (see `emitDegradeGate` and `INT64_HELPER`). The two
that remain baked are the pattern queries, which are rational arithmetic over a
mini-notation tree — an interpreter, not a formula, and a different kind of
problem. There is nothing to lower symbolically even in principle: a
`PatPattern` is a `(PatArc) -> List<PatEvent>` lambda, so the emitter cannot tell
a `"bd*4"` from a `sine` from the outside, let alone find a closed form for it.
They go through `bakeTrack`, and what that costs depends on the track:

- a **rhythm** is piecewise constant, so the bake is exact except for where its
  edges are, and each edge is bisected to `BAKE_EDGE_TOLERANCE` — a microsecond,
  the same order as the millionth of a cycle [`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack) quantises its own queries
  to, which is the resolution the edge exists at in the first place;
- a **signal** — `sine`, `tri`, `perlin` — has no plateaus and no exactness to
  claim, so both a hold chain and a ramp through the samples are built and the one
  that measures closer wins. That is the ramp by 100x to 3000x, except on `saw`
  and `isaw`, whose once-a-cycle wrap a straight line would smear;
- `rand` is neither. It hashes the reduced rational instant it is handed, so it
  has no value *between* samples: a finer bake is a different signal, not a better
  approximation of this one. The emitter detects that by baking it twice — halving
  the rate leaves the error where it was — says so, and stops claiming otherwise.

Which of the three, and what it measured, is [`RectSLSdfResult.bakes`](languages.md#rectslglsl-kt--rectslsdfresult--bakes); the same
thing as a sentence is [`RectSLSdfResult.notes`](languages.md#rectslglsl-kt--rectslsdfresult--notes). `RectSLSdfBakeTest` measures each
regime on the timeline, and `RectSLGlslSdfTest` holds the whole gallery to the
bound its own classification implies.

## RectSLImg.kt { #rectslimg-kt }

A RectSL scene as a sequence of [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img)s: the bridge from the rectangle language to everything in
Field that reads an image — `afield.media.image` filters, `showImg`, and `Patch.mapImage`, which puts
a scene on a light rig.

Frames come from the CPU reference rasterizer the RectSL study tools use
([`CpuRectSLRasterizer`](languages.md#rectslstudyrender-kt-cpurectslrasterizer)), so no window or graphics context is needed: the scene's background, its
rectangles blended as the GPU blends them into an 8-bit target, and its StackSL materials run
through the StackSL GLSL interpreter. One sample per pixel, at the pixel's centre; the wall fills
the frame whatever its `->fit` says, row 0 at the top of the wall.

The source is compiled once, here, including any `{{ … }}` Kotlin escapes; a scene that does not
compile throws, naming its errors.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val scene = RectSLImager(source)
val img = scene.frame(1.5, 256, 128)          // the colours as typed, 0..1
patch.mapImage(img.resize(16, 8))             // one fixture per cell, area-averaged
```

**sRGB or light.** By default a frame holds the colours *as typed*: `0x808080` is 0.502, which is
what the RectSL pictures show and what an 8-bit target stores. Pass `linear = true` for the light
those values stand for (0.216 for that grey). Averaging, blurring or down-sizing a frame is only
physically right on linear values, and an LED's PWM is linear in light; so a rig driven from a
linear frame at gamma 1 and a rig driven from an as-typed frame at `withGamma(2.2)` both show
roughly the right brightness, but only the first averages a thin line to the right energy.

## RectSLPattern.kt { #rectslpattern-kt }

### RectSL's musical layer — the Tidal pattern language as scene structure

RectSL already had *time*: tracks, `->live birth life`, `->stagger-time`, `->split`. What it
did not have was **meter** — a shared clock, subdivision, and (the one that actually matters)
any way for repetition *n+1* to differ from repetition *n*. The array primitives distribute
copies in space and every copy plays the same clip. That is the difference between a loop and
a groove, and it is exactly the gap `afield.audio.synth`'s pattern language fills.

The two languages turn out to be the same shape underneath, which is why this bridge is thin
rather than a translation layer:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
RectSL   interface Track<out T> { fun sample(t: Double): T }
Pattern  class PatPattern<A>    { fun events(arc: PatArc): List<PatEvent<A>> }
```

Both are **pure functions of time**, queryable out of order, with no simulation state —
`PatContractTest`'s purity and query-order properties assert it on one side, and RectSL's
closed-form tracks (the reason `HeadingTrack` can recover velocity by finite difference)
assert it on the other. So composing them needs no scheduler and no frame loop: a pattern
*is* a track ([`PatTrack`](languages.md#rectslpattern-kt-pattrack)), and an event *is* a life window (`patArray`).

#### What lives here

| § | words |
| --- | --- |
| clock | `->cps` `->tempo` `->beats-per-cycle` `->duration-cycles` `beats` `cycles` `cycle-secs` |
| pat | `pat` and its per-event context `t` `dur` `cyc` `step` `atom` `param` `param?` |
| patterns as values | `mini` `sine` `cosine` `saw` `isaw` `tri` `square` `rand` `perlin` `nums` `texts` `segment` `pat-range` `quantise` `bipolar` `euclid` `kolakoski` `kolakoski-gaps` |
| variation | `->every` `->off` `->jux` `->degrade` `->swing` `->press` `->iter` `->chunk` |
| layout | `strip` `->euclid` `->kolakoski` |
| out | `pat-events` |

#### Why a separate file

RectSL.kt is already 4.6k lines, and this layer is the only part of the language that depends
on `afield.audio.synth`. Keeping the dependency in one file means the rest of RectSL still
compiles and reads without knowing the pattern language exists. What it reaches back into
RectSL.kt for is a short list: `RectLangVm.word`/`RectLangVm.mutator`
(so the musical words register through the same one path as every other word),
`RectLangVm.loopStack` and [`LoopFrame.pat`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--loopframe--pat) (so `i`/`n`/`f` keep working inside a `pat` body),
`SceneBuilder.mapScalarTracks`, and [`SceneBuilder.cps`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--scenebuilder--cps).

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DegradeGateTrack</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">ordinal</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">probability</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">cps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">salt</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Track</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSLPatternOps/#L70)

Deterministic per-object, per-cycle dropout — the visual `degradeBy`. The same scene always drops the same copies on the same cycles, which is the point: a groove you cannot reproduce is not a groove. The hash is a plain integer mix rather than [`afield.audio.synth.rand`](patterns.md#patsignals-kt--rand) because it is keyed on *object ordinal* and cycle, not on a rational time instant.

## RectSLSdfLook.kt { #rectslsdflook-kt }

What to *do* with a RectSL distance field once you have one.

[`RectSLGlsl.emitSdf`](languages.md#rectslglsl-kt--rectslglsl--emitsdf) answers a single question per point — how far to the
nearest visible rectangle, at this instant — and its KDoc lists what that
buys: outlines and glows at any width, blending between rectangles, boolean
ops, per-pixel normals, sub-frame motion blur. Each of those is a handful of
GLSL lines over the same `float`, and writing them once per demo is how a
capability stays a claim. This file is the vocabulary instead: a look is data,
[`RectSLSdfShader`](languages.md#rectslsdflook-kt-rectslsdfshader) turns `(field, look)` into a complete fragment shader, and
`RectSLSdfLook.PRESETS` is one worked example of every advertised capability.

### What is a look and what is not

Two of the capabilities are *not* looks, and the split matters. Smooth-union
between rects changes the set itself, so it happens in the emitter
([`RectSLSdfOptions.blendRadius`](languages.md#rectslglsl-kt--rectslsdfoptions--blendradius)) — a look can only carry the number and hand
it over. Boolean subtraction needs a *second* field, so a carving look is only
meaningful when the caller supplies one; [`RectSLSdfShader.fragment`](languages.md#rectslsdflook-kt--rectslsdfshader--fragment) requires
it and says so.

### Why the edges are measured in pixels

Every softness here is expressed as a multiple of one screen pixel, recovered
per-fragment with `fwidth` on the world coordinate. That is the whole point of
a distance field over a rasterized quad: the same scene at 512px and at 4096px
has one-pixel edges at both, and no geometry was re-tessellated to get there.
Widths that describe the *scene* rather than the screen — an outline's
thickness, a contour's spacing, a bevel's depth — are in wall units, because
those are properties of the drawing and should zoom with it.

## RectSLSimplify.kt { #rectslsimplify-kt }

An algebraic simplifier over the track IR, under a requirement that every rewrite be bit-exact.

The IR is data classes, so two tracks built by the same `array` body compare `==`. The GLSL
emitter's function deduplication rests on that, keying emitted functions by the track itself so
that a hundred array copies share one function, and so does the `min(x, x)` rule below, which
compares two subtrees directly. The narrower rewrites over the same IR are `describe()`, which
prints a track, and `substituteParameters`, which sets named free parameters to numbers; this is
the general one.

Nothing in `afield.lang.rectsl` writes a track out or reads one back, so a track cannot be
serialized, although being data rather than closures would allow it.

### What it is for

Not speed, primarily. RectSL's array words build per-copy channels by *offsetting* a constant, so a
hundred-copy array arrives at a backend as a hundred `BinaryDoubleTrack(const, const, ADD)` nodes,
and each backend has had to fold that itself: `trackConstantValue` exists because the GLSL emitter
needed it, and the `Fn` lowering calls the same function for the same reason. A fold is the
*smallest* rewrite there is, and both emitters had to reach for it themselves because there
was nowhere over the IR to apply it once.

The bigger reason is that a simplified tree is a smaller `Fn` graph, and an `Fn` graph's size is
the cost of both a sample and a gradient — `Fn.eval` walks every node, and `gradientAt` records
every node on a tape. A fit runs that thousands of times.

### The contract: every rule is bit-exact

A simplified track must sample **bit-identically** to the original, not merely equal-to-tolerance,
which rules out several rewrites everyone writes by reflex. The gallery corpus caught the first
one: `0 - x` rewritten to `-x` disagrees at `x = 0`, because `0.0 - 0.0` is `+0.0` and `-(0.0)`
is `-0.0`.

A signed zero is not a curiosity in this IR. [`HeadingTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-headingtrack) takes `atan2` of a velocity, and
`atan2(+0.0, -1.0)` is `+pi` while `atan2(-0.0, -1.0)` is `-pi` — half a turn apart. A rewrite that
"only" changes the sign of a zero can therefore spin a rectangle through 180 degrees. So the rules
kept here are the ones exact for every double including both zeros, and the reflexive ones are
dropped with their reasons:

| rewrite | kept? | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| constant folding | yes | exact by construction — the folded value *is* what the chain evaluated to |
| `x - 0` -> `x` | yes | `x - (+0.0) == x` for every x, both zeros included |
| `x * 1`, `x / 1`, `x ^ 1` | yes | multiplicative identity preserves sign |
| `min(x, x)`, `max(x, x)` -> `x` | yes | structural equality; exact whatever x is |
| `-(-x)` -> `x`, `abs abs`, `saturate saturate` | yes | involution / idempotence, sign-exact |
| `clamp(x, v, v)` -> `v` | yes | `coerceIn(x, v, v)` is `v` |
| `shift 0`, `scale 1`, degenerate `loop`/`pingpong` | yes | the lookup is `t` unchanged |
| `x + 0` -> `x` | **no** | `(-0.0) + 0.0` is `+0.0`, so this flips a signed zero |
| `0 - x` -> `-x` | **no** | the rule the corpus caught, above |
| `mix(a, b, 1)` -> `b` | **no** | `a + (b - a)` is not `b` in floating point at all |
| `mix(a, b, 0)` -> `a`, `mix(a, a, t)` -> `a` | **no** | both end in `a + (+/-0.0)`, signed-zero unsafe |
| `x * 0` -> `0` | **no** | only valid for finite x, and nothing here proves x is finite |

Losing the additive identity costs less than it looks like it should: RectSL's array words build
per-copy channels by *offsetting a constant*, and the constant fold takes those whole.

Free parameters are never folded, for the same reason `trackConstantValue` takes a flag: a
[`FreeParamTrack`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-freeparamtrack) holds a number but is not *a* number, and folding it away would delete the
thing a fit is meant to solve for.

### How it is checked

`RectSLSimplifyTest` runs it over the gallery and requires every rewritten channel to sample
**bit-identically** to the original at 41 times each, and to be a fixed point of a second pass.
The node-count reduction it prints is reported rather than asserted at any figure, because that
figure moves with the gallery and with the IR — a key value became a node when [`TcbKey`](languages.md#rectsl-kt-tcbkey) began
holding a track, for instance. Run the test to read the current one.

A plausible-looking rule that is wrong in one corner is this file's characteristic failure, and
bit-identity over the corpus already assembled for the differentiable backend is what catches it.

## RectSLSoftRaster.kt { #rectslsoftraster-kt }

The third lowering: a RectSL scene as a **differentiable raster**, so a picture can be fitted.

### Why an image fit needs a rasterizer

[`Track.fitParameters`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt--fitparameters) turns the arrow round for one *track*: mark a number `free-param`, say what
the track should read at three instants, and the exact gradient of the lowered `Fn` walks the
number to the answer. What it cannot do is take a *target image*, because the derivative an image
fit needs is `d(pixel)/d(parameter)` and a per-track scalar lowering has no pixels in it. That was
recognised on 2026-08-06 and the image fit was abandoned rather than half-landed. This file is the
retry, on the terms the abandonment set: a soft rasterizer **whose coverage bias is measured**.
The exact reference that bias is measured against is `exactCoverage`; the numbers, and where they
say this is and is not usable, are in `dev_docs/RECTSL_SOFT_RASTER.md`.

### The one design decision worth arguing about

The obvious plan is "lower the scene to an `Fn`-valued signed distance field over (x, y, t)".
[`Functions.Fn`](math.md#functions-kt--functions--fn) cannot be that: it is a `(Double) -> Double`, one input and one output, and every
existing consumer of a lowered track — [`freeParameterSlots`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt--sceneadfield--freeparameterslots), [`Track.substituteParameters`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt--substituteparameters),
[`Track.fitParameters`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt--fitparameters) — reads its θ-vector as *the track's own leaves*. Smuggling x and y in as two
more θ leaves would make all of them wrong about what they are solving for, and nothing would
report it.

So the differentiable layer here is not `Fn`, it is [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) on an [`ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape) — which is what `Fn`'s own
gradient is built out of anyway. `FnAutoDiff.interpret` already re-reads an `Fn` graph in `AD`
arithmetic at an `AD`-tracked x, so:

- every **track** goes through the existing lowering, [`Track.toFn`](languages.md#rectslfn-kt--tofn), unchanged;
- every track is then *interpreted* on the tape at the frame's time;
- the **geometry** — the ancestor-group composition, the rotate-into-local-frame, the exact box
  field, the `min` union — is written in `AD` directly, transcribed from the GLSL in
  [`RectSLGlsl.PRELUDE`](languages.md#rectslglsl-kt--rectslglsl--prelude) and the composition in [`Transform2d.then`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--transform2d--then);
- the **coverage kernel** and the **image loss** go on the same tape.

One backward sweep then yields `d(loss)/dθ` for every parameter in the scene at once, with nothing
finite-differenced anywhere in the chain. That is strictly more than an `Fn` could have given.

### The scene-level θ ledger

[`Track.fitParameters`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt--fitparameters) masks θ within **one** `Fn`. A scene has eight tracks per rect and 183 rects
in the largest gallery scene, so it has hundreds of independent θ-vectors, and "index *i*" means
nothing until they are concatenated. [`SceneAdField`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-sceneadfield) does that concatenation once: every channel
gets a contiguous block, [`SceneAdField.theta`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt--sceneadfield--theta) is the whole scene's leaves in block order, and
[`SceneAdField.freeParameterSlots`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt--sceneadfield--freeparameterslots) re-maps each `free-param` **name** to its *global* slots —
unioned across channels, because one name legitimately reaches several of them. The
gradient-summed, step-applied-to-every-slot discipline of [`Track.fitParameters`](languages.md#rectslfit-kt--fitparameters) carries over
unchanged; only the index space is new.

### Why a frame is a separate object

[`ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape) records five parallel arrays per operation and never shrinks. A 128² raster over a
30-rect scene, naively taped, is ~14M nodes — half a gigabyte. But a shape's *transform* depends
only on (θ, t) and not on the pixel, so [`SceneAdField.frameAt`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt--sceneadfield--frameat) evaluates all of it once and
[`SceneAdFrame`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt-sceneadframe) hands back only what varies per pixel: centre, rotation, half-extent, alpha. The
per-pixel cost drops to about twenty tape nodes per rect, and because an image loss is a *sum*
over pixels its gradient is additive — so [`softRasterLossAndGradient`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt--softrasterlossandgradient) walks the image in row
chunks, one tape per chunk, and accumulates. Memory becomes a choice rather than a limit.

### Fidelity between the two interpreters

A second interpreter of the same graph is exactly the situation where a *slightly different
function* gets differentiated confidently. `autodiff_fn.kt` has a name for the guard against that
— [`FnAutoDiff.worstValueDisagreement`](function.md#autodiff-fn-kt--fnautodiff--worstvaluedisagreement) — and [`toAdField`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt--toadfield) runs it on every channel it lowers,
recording the worst in [`SceneAdField.worstChannelDisagreement`](languages.md#rectslsoftraster-kt--sceneadfield--worstchanneldisagreement). A channel whose `AD` reading parts
company with its own `Fn.eval` is refused, not averaged in.

## RectSLSoftRasterFigure.kt { #rectslsoftrasterfigure-kt }

A soft raster, its exact reference, and the difference between them — as a picture.

The third panel is `|soft - exact|` on a heat ramp, with its own peak printed in the corner. It
shows *where* a soft raster's bias lives: a thin fringe along an oblique edge, a bright bar down a
union seam, a whole feature glowing when it is thinner than the band.

The figure is a CPU raster, for the reason [`RectSLFitFigure`](languages.md#rectslfitfigure-kt-rectslfitfigure) gives: per-pixel coverage is the data
here, so a GPU would add only a device, a window and a render target. The labels use the same 3×5
dot-matrix font RectSL's own plotting words use.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSLSoftRasterFigure.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSLSoftRasterFigure/)

## RectSLSource.kt { #rectslsource-kt }

RectSL read as *source*: what the editor and the study tools need that a plain compile does not
give — where things are.

[`compileRectSL`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--compilerectsl) answers "does it compile, and to what". A person editing a scene, or a model
talking one into existence, also needs to know *which line* a problem is on, *which line* made a
given rectangle, and *which numbers* in the text are worth turning. The tokenizer records where each
token began ([`RectLangTokenizer.offsets`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--rectlangtokenizer--offsets)), the evaluator records what it was evaluating when it
failed ([`RectLangVm.failedAt`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--rectlangvm--failedat)), and the scene reports each node as it is made
(`SceneBuilder.onNode`); this file turns those into lines.

Nothing here changes what a program means: [`compileRectSLWithSource`](languages.md#rectslsource-kt--compilerectslwithsource) runs the same tokenizer and
evaluator as [`compileRectSL`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--compilerectsl), with the same curves, engine and pre-compiled escapes.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSLSource.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSLSource/)

## RectSLVocabulary.kt { #rectslvocabulary-kt }

Every word the RectSL evaluator knows, with what the cheatsheet says it does — the vocabulary the
editor offers in completion and explains beside the cursor.

The words are the evaluator's own ([`RectLangVm.wordMetadata`](languages.md#rectsl-kt--rectlangvm--wordmetadata), the set its "did you mean"
searches), so a word the evaluator knows is offered even when the editor's hand-written table
(`rectsl.js`) lacks it. Their stack effect and description come from the RectSL words guide, which
`tools/rectsl_conversation_documents.py` generates from `public/docs/rectsl_cheatsheet.md` and holds
equal to it. The editor asks for completion through Field's `complete` request, which a RectSL
scene answers here ([RectSLExecution](languages.md#rectslprograms-kt-rectslexecution)), as does a Kotlin box for
its `rectSL` property.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSLVocabulary.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/RectSLVocabulary/)

## RectslBoxTools.kt { #rectslboxtools-kt }

Two tools a document can hand to its AI4 agents: one syntax-checks a RectSL program, the other
renders it in the document's live Field 4 window and returns the captured frames to the
conversation.

Both are built with [`aiTool`](machine-learning.md#boxaitools-kt--aitool). A box registers the pair once in its `code`, and running that
again replaces them:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
registerRectslStudioTools()
```
The agent then sees `rectsl.check` and `rectsl.run`. `{{ … }}` escapes in the RectSL source are
compiled against *this box's* Kotlin engine, so they can read the box's live state (ki-vars,
`thisBox` members).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/rectsl/RectslBoxTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/RectslBoxTools/)

## RectSLPrograms.kt { #rectslprograms-kt }

RectSL as a main language in Field: running a scene box compiles its `rectSL`, draws it live in the
window above it, and checks it in to the box's study.

[`RectSLPrograms`](languages.md#rectslprograms-kt-rectslprograms) holds the per-box studies, [`RectSLLive`](languages.md#rectslprograms-kt-rectsllive) keeps a box's window following its edits,
[`RectSLExecution`](languages.md#rectslprograms-kt-rectslexecution) is the box execution, and the `install...` functions register the language, its line
notes, its topology watcher and its scene action.

## RectSLStudy.kt { #rectslstudy-kt }

The RectSL study: checked revisions of a box's `rectSL` scene, and the frames, timelines, traces,
knob sweeps, variants and comparisons that an AI4 chat and a person use to look at it.

The file holds [`RectSLStudy`](languages.md#rectslstudy-kt-rectslstudy) itself, the [`RectSLCheck`](languages.md#rectslstudy-kt-rectslcheck) and [`RectSLLineReport`](languages.md#rectslstudy-kt-rectsllinereport) results it returns,
and [`RectSLEscapes`](languages.md#rectslstudy-kt-rectslescapes).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/rectsl/study/RectSLStudy.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/study/RectSLStudy/)

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">RectSLEscapes</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/study/RectSLStudy/#L1326)

`{{ … }}` Kotlin escapes for study and runtime compiles: each distinct escape is compiled to its lambda once, on a dedicated Kotlin engine created on first use, and reused by every later compile. Not the box's own engine — a box engine busy running code would be re-entered — and never on Field's main thread, which a compile could block.

### RectSLRasterizer { #rectslstudyrender-kt-rectslrasterizer }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">typealias</span> <span class="nc">RectSLRasterizer</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StudyFrames</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">RectSLDrawable</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/study/RectSLStudyRender/#L205)

Where a RectSL study's frames come from: the GPU when a window is running ([`RectSLGpuRasterizer`](languages.md#rectslstudyrender-kt-rectslgpurasterizer)), the CPU reference when it is not ([`CpuRectSLRasterizer`](languages.md#rectslstudyrender-kt-cpurectslrasterizer)). Both return linear colour, rows top to bottom, the wall filling the frame. A [`StudyFrames`](workspace.md#studyframes-kt-studyframes) of a compiled scene.

### CpuRectSLRasterizer { #rectslstudyrender-kt-cpurectslrasterizer }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">CpuRectSLRasterizer</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RectSLRasterizer</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/rectsl/study/RectSLStudyRender/#L215)

The CPU reference: the lowered mesh rasterized quad by quad at pixel centres, blended as the GPU blends into its 8-bit target (source alpha over, on the typed values), shaded as [`RectSLStudyShader.fragment`](languages.md#rectslstudyrender-kt--rectslstudyshader--fragment) shades — the three built-in materials in Kotlin, a StackSL material through the StackSL GLSL interpreter — and decoded to linear light at the end, as the GPU's bytes are. It needs no graphics context, so tests and headless runs see the scene the window shows, a few levels apart at rectangle edges (it samples one point per pixel, with a top-left fill rule like the GPU's).

## RectSLStudyTools.kt { #rectslstudytools-kt }

The tools an AI4 conversation gets when it is opened on a RectSL scene's `rectSL` property.

Each works on the focused box's own study (see [`RectSLPrograms`](languages.md#rectslprograms-kt-rectslprograms)), so nothing here is per
document. A document can still add tools of its own from a box: [`AgentToolExtensions.register`](machine-learning.md#agenttoolextensions-kt--agenttoolextensions--register)
with its document as the scope.

## Asta.kt { #asta-kt }

Source-to-source rewriting of a JavaScript box, over Nashorn's parse tree.

JavaScript has no operator overloading, so in a RemoteJS box `a + b` on two vectors concatenates
their string forms and `a - b` is `NaN`. This pass rewrites the source before it ships: each
binary `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `^` becomes a call to a global named for the operator, so `a + b`
leaves here as `__PLUS__(a,b)`. The head supplies those globals in `field/asta.js`, where
`__PLUS__`, `__MINUS__`, `__MULTIPLY__` and `__DIVIDE__` work componentwise on `THREE` vectors,
promote an array of two or three numbers to a vector first, let an operand join the protocol by
defining its own `__PLUS__` (or `__RPLUS__`, for the right-hand side), and throw a named error
where plain JavaScript would hand back `NaN` or `"[object Object]"`. `XOR` is in the trap set
here and has no counterpart there.

`executeRemoteJS` runs the pass when its `doASTA` flag is set, which is the default. The
Kotlin/JS path sets it false, because Kotlin has `operator fun plus` of its own and a compiled
box needs no rewriting.

The pass also recovers a source location. Nashorn parses at ES6 while the browser is the
authority on whether newer syntax is valid, so a diagnostic raised here is held rather than
shown, and used only to fill in the line and column of a `SyntaxError` that the head reported
without one; an error the head raises at run time keeps its own location. A parser
`AssertionError` is caught, notified, and the source returned unrewritten, so a construct
Nashorn cannot read costs the operators rather than the run.

Rewriting is textual, so offsets do the work, and Nashorn's need correcting before they can
index the string. A string literal's quotes fall outside its reported extent, and a node that
reports a narrower span than its own children is widened to cover them. Replacements run
back-to-front so an earlier edit cannot move a later one, and the header of a `for` loop is
excluded from rewriting entirely, because an edit inside it shifts the offsets of everything the
loop spans. Field's `//# sourceURL=` trailer is split off before parsing and appended again
afterwards.

`Options` gates the whole pass. `overloads` is on, and is the operator rewrite above; `numbers`
is off, and rewrites each numeric literal to `__NUMBER_LITERAL__(start, end, text)`, for which
this tree carries no head-side definition; `functionRewrite` is off and has no effect beyond
making the pass run at all. With all three off, `parseAndReconstruct` returns its input
unchanged.

## KotlinJs.kt { #kotlinjs-kt }

SPIKE — a "Kotlin in the head" main language. A box flagged `mainLanguage = "kotlinjs"` (or its
legacy [`isKotlinJsRoot`](languages.md#kotlinjs-kt--iskotlinjsroot) root flag) compiles its Kotlin source to JavaScript via
[`KotlinToJsCompiler`](languages.md#kotlintojscompiler-kt-kotlintojscompiler) (PLAIN_DCE: self-contained, tree-shaken, eval-able) and ships it to the
connected browser / visionOS head over the same WebSocket transport RemoteJS uses.

This reuses RemoteJS's transport wholesale ([`compileAndSendKotlin`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--compileandsendkotlin) → [`executeRemoteJS`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--executeremotejs) with
`doASTA = false`); it only swaps *what runs the box* (Kotlin→JS compile) for the JS path. Kotlin
gets native operator overloading (no ASTA), real types, and compile-time diagnostics at the
source line. See dev_docs/kotlin_to_js_spike.md.

## KotlinJsBinding.kt { #kotlinjsbinding-kt }

One source of truth for a Kotlin/JS façade surface.

A KotlinJS head profile needs the *same* API described twice: once as compiler-facing `external`
declarations (the JS target the box compiles against) and once as a JVM-analysis-safe mirror (what
the out-of-process K2 Analysis-API completion sidecar analyzes — it has no `dynamic`, and `external`
declarations behave differently there). Maintaining those two by hand drifts — e.g. a property
that's `var` in one and `val` in the other, or a member completion offers that compilation rejects.

So describe the surface ONCE with [`jsBinding`](languages.md#kotlinjsbinding-kt--jsbinding) and let [`JsBindingModel.compilerDeclarations`](languages.md#kotlinjsbinding-kt--jsbindingmodel--compilerdeclarations) and
[`JsBindingModel.completionDeclarations`](languages.md#kotlinjsbinding-kt--jsbindingmodel--completiondeclarations) render both. The two rendered forms differ only mechanically:

| aspect            | compiler (`external`)      | completion (plain, JVM-analysis) |
|-------------------|----------------------------|----------------------------------|
| declaration       | `external object/class`    | plain `object/class`             |
| member fun body   | none                       | `= TODO()`                       |
| property init     | none                       | `= <init>` (default `TODO()`)    |
| ctor param default| `= definedExternally`      | `= <real default>`               |
| supertype         | `: Base`                   | `: Base()`                       |
| `dynamic`         | `dynamic`                  | `Any?`                           |
| callback type     | `() -> Unit`               | `Function0<Unit>`                |
| operator/fun body | real body                  | `= TODO()`                       |

A field that is both a constructor argument and a mutable property (THREE's `Vector3(x,y,z)` with
mutable `.x/.y/.z`, or `Mesh(geometry, material)` with mutable `.geometry/.material`) is one
[`TypeBuilder.field`](languages.md#kotlinjsbinding-kt--typebuilder--field) call — it emits a plain ctor param plus a `var` property in BOTH renderings,
so the two can never disagree on mutability or on whether the property exists.

## KotlinJsHeadProfiles.kt { #kotlinjsheadprofiles-kt }

Which remote head a Kotlin/JS box runs on, chosen by a marker on its first line.

A box whose main language is `kotlinjs` compiles to JavaScript and ships to a head over the
RemoteJS transport, but the heads are not interchangeable: each has a different set of globals
loaded, and Kotlin can only be typed against the globals its target actually has. A profile is
that pairing. It carries the `external` declarations spliced in front of the author's source
before compiling, a second surface used for completion, and the transport and lifecycle calls
that put the compiled JavaScript in front of a head.

`KotlinJsHeadProfiles.resolve` reads a `// {{ name }}` marker on the first non-blank line and
returns a [`KotlinJsHeadSelection`](languages.md#kotlinjsheadprofiles-kt-kotlinjsheadselection). A name is matched case-insensitively against an id or an
alias:

 - `remote` — the plain RemoteJS head; aliases `default` and `remotejs`, and what a box with no
   marker at all gets.
 - `remoteAR` — the A-Frame and THREE scene head; aliases `ar`, `remote-ar`, `remotear`.
 - `tone` — the Tone.js computer-music head; aliases `tonejs` and `music`.
 - `visionmetal` — the visionOS Metal head; aliases `metal` and `vision-metal`.

An unknown name raises instead of falling back, because a box compiled against the wrong globals
type-checks and then fails in the head. The same reasoning gates delivery at run time: a head
has to report the capability keys its profile requires in its `initialize` payload before it is
counted or sent to, so `// {{ tone }}` reaches a head with Tone loaded and no other.

Two further things `resolve` does, both about line numbers. It blanks the marker's line rather
than removing it, so the lines the compiler reports still line up with what the author sees. And
`resolveForBox` re-reads the marker from the box's stored `code` when the source handed to it
carries none, which is what fragment and symbol execution pass when only a selection is being
run.

The two implementations behind the sealed class mean different things by sending. The WebSocket
one hands its JavaScript to `executeRemoteJS` with `doASTA = false`, broadcasts to every
connected head that matches, and reports results back through the box's output. The visionOS one
publishes a Metal program on the box instead and reports success without waiting, because that
publication is durable and replays for a native head that subscribes later. Its `uniforms`
option is the only marker option here: slot order is what the head turns into `#define u_NAME`,
so it is declared rather than inferred, and the inference that covers an absent declaration says
what it guessed.

## KotlinJsSourceMap.kt { #kotlinjssourcemap-kt }

The source map of a Kotlin→JS box's compiled module, remembered per box so that output arriving
after the run can still be given a line.

The map is a by-product of the compile, and the output that needs it usually arrives once the run
has finished: an error from a timer, a `console.log` from an event handler, each carrying a line of
generated JavaScript and nothing else. `RemoteJS.kt` builds a map the moment [`KotlinToJsCompiler`](languages.md#kotlintojscompiler-kt-kotlintojscompiler)
returns one and remembers it under the box id; `KotlinJsHeadProfiles.kt` asks for it when a reply
needs a line; the next compile of that box replaces it.

None of this reports a failure to the box. A compile that produced no map, or a map whose
`mappings` the decoder rejects, leaves the box with none, and its output keeps the generated line
it came with. A position that maps somewhere other than the box's own Kotlin is a null from
[`editorLine`](languages.md#kotlinjssourcemap-kt--kotlinjssourcemap--editorline), and [`editorLineForStack`](languages.md#kotlinjssourcemap-kt--kotlinjssourcemap--editorlineforstack) goes on to the next frame of the stack.
