## KotlinToJsCompiler.kt { #kotlintojscompiler-kt }

SPIKE — Kotlin source -> JavaScript, for RemoteJS boxes.

This mirrors what JetBrains' `kotlin-compiler-server` (KotlinToJSTranslator) does: a two-phase
K2 compile of a self-contained Kotlin snippet into a single, eval-able JS module that the existing
RemoteJS transport ships to the browser / visionOS "graphics head" over the WebSocket bus.

    phase 1:  source.kt      --( -Xir-produce-klib-file )-->                 <module>.klib
    phase 2:  <module>.klib  --( -Xir-produce-js, -Xinclude, -Xir-dce )-->   <module>.js

What this buys a box author is Kotlin: real types, completion, and native `operator fun plus`
vector and matrix math, so a Kotlin box needs none of the operator rewriting `Asta.kt` does for a
JavaScript one. The result runs unchanged in the head via `executeRemoteJS` with
`doASTA = false`.

Output is a `plain` module that self-invokes `main`, so the head's `global.eval(code)` runs it
with no changes. Dead-code elimination is what keeps that module small enough to ship on every
compile: it tree-shakes the stdlib, taking a trivial program well under the ~600 KB an
unshaken one contributes, and `KotlinToJsSpikeTest` holds the emitted JS under 50 000
characters.

Two execution modes (`Mode`):
 - IN_PROCESS: calls `K2JSCompiler().exec(...)` directly, with no JVM launch to pay for. The K2
   REPL (`KotlinInterface2`) already holds a live IntelliJ application environment in this JVM
   and `K2JSCompiler` reuses the process-wide `getOrCreateApplicationEnvironment`; the two
   coexist, and a throw from that call falls back to SUBPROCESS rather than failing the compile.
 - SUBPROCESS: spawns `java -cp <this app's classpath> K2JSCompiler`. Fully isolated, and reuses
   the embeddable compiler already on the runtime classpath. Slower, by a cold JVM per compile.

Follow-up (see dev_docs/kotlin_to_js_spike.md): incremental compiles via JsIrCompilerWithIC, and a
typed `external` façade over the head runtime (THREE / A-Frame / Field JS).

## RemoteArKotlinJs.kt { #remotearkotlinjs-kt }

The Kotlin/JS declarations a box sees when it runs Kotlin in the browser RemoteAR head.

[`RemoteArKotlinJs`](languages.md#remotearkotlinjs-kt-remotearkotlinjs) describes the `THREE` globals the `extensions/remote_ar` head installs
(scene objects, vectors, FLine construction, the stage proxy and the animation task loop) with
[`jsBinding`](languages.md#kotlinjsbinding-kt--jsbinding). From that one description it produces [`RemoteArKotlinJs.declarations`](languages.md#remotearkotlinjs-kt--remotearkotlinjs--declarations), the
`external` declarations the Kotlin/JS compiler sees, and [`RemoteArKotlinJs.completionDeclarations`](languages.md#remotearkotlinjs-kt--remotearkotlinjs--completiondeclarations),
the stub model the completion sidecar analyses on the JVM. It also adds FLine operators
(`fline + rotate(0.5)`, `fline * 2.0`) and named scene slots (`SCENE`name` = obj`).

## RemoteJS.kt { #remotejs-kt }

RemoteJS — JavaScript that runs in a *browser somewhere else*, written in a Field box here.

The value proposition is not "Field can run JavaScript". It is that the box is on this machine and
the execution is on a **head**: a browser tab, an Electron window, a phone, a Vision Pro. A head
connects inbound over the WebSocket Field already has, announces an id and its capabilities, and
from then on a box can be pointed at one head, at all of them, or at a filtered subset.
[`knownOpenRemoteClients`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--knownopenremoteclients) and [`remoteClientCapabilities`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--remoteclientcapabilities) are that registry, keyed by head id, and
they are the reason nearly everything here takes a `filterSession` rather than a connection.

### The one function to read

[`executeRemoteJS`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--executeremotejs) is the language. Its parameter list *is* the semantics, and three of them carry
most of the weight:

 - `doASTA` routes the source through [`Asta`](languages.md#asta-kt-asta) first, which rewrites each binary operator into a
   call the head's `asta.js` defines, so vector arithmetic in a box means what it looks like.
   That pass also parses, and its diagnostics fill in the line and column of a `SyntaxError` the
   browser reported without one; an error raised at run time keeps its own location. Turn it
   off, as the Kotlin/JS path does, and a box gets neither.
 - `lifecycleName` and `launchable` are what make a fragment restartable and time-scrubbable
   rather than fire-and-forget, and `timeStart`/`timeEnd` are the window it is live for.
 - `handleTo` is the return channel: a head can send values back, dispatched through
   [`returnHandlers`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--returnhandlers), so this is a duplex language and not a one-way pipe.

[`RemoteJSExectution`](languages.md#remotejs-kt-remotejsexectution) is the `BoxExecution` for a box written *in* JavaScript;
[`installRemoteJSMainLanguage`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--installremotejsmainlanguage) registers it, and [`becomeRemote`](languages.md#remotejs-kt--becomeremote) is the imperative version for a
box that is being converted. Note the two ids: this file registers `remotejs`, and `KotlinJs.kt`
beside it registers `kotlinjs` — the same transport, but the box is written in Kotlin and
cross-compiled, with `KotlinToJsCompiler.kt` doing the compiling and
[`afield.lang.remotejs.KotlinJsHeadProfile`](languages.md#kotlinjsheadprofiles-kt-kotlinjsheadprofile) describing what each kind of head can be asked to do. Two
main languages, one package.

`dev_docs/small_language_anatomy.md` is the map of the integration points every main language
touches.

## RemoteJsBoxSurface.kt { #remotejsboxsurface-kt }

Where a message from a browser head lands when it names a box rather than a run.

A head reaches Field over the WebSocket Field already has, and every message it sends carries an
address. `RemoteJS.kt`'s dispatcher tries those addresses in turn and [`handle`](languages.md#remotejsboxsurface-kt--remotejsboxsurface--handle) is its last
claimant, so a `false` from here is what makes a message unrecognised. What reaches it is whatever
the head has to say about a box while no reply channel is open: `display`, the `slider` and
`checkbox` a box asked for, and output a timer or an event handler printed after the run returned.
A Kotlin→JS box arrives here as well, and [`routeLateOutput`](languages.md#remotejsboxsurface-kt--remotejsboxsurface--routelateoutput) maps its generated-JavaScript line back
to the editor on the way through.

None of those messages carries a box, only the code name the head evaluated the source under.
[`handle`](languages.md#remotejsboxsurface-kt--remotejsboxsurface--handle) and [`routeLateOutput`](languages.md#remotejsboxsurface-kt--remotejsboxsurface--routelateoutput) resolve it through [`boxFor`](languages.md#remotejsboxsurface-kt--remotejsboxsurface--boxfor), and take that lookup as a parameter so
a test can supply a box directly.

In the other direction this file writes JavaScript as text for the transport to evaluate in the
head: [`stopScript`](languages.md#remotejsboxsurface-kt--remotejsboxsurface--stopscript) when a box is stopped, [`controlScript`](languages.md#remotejsboxsurface-kt--remotejsboxsurface--controlscript) when a control drawn here is moved.
`dev_docs/REMOTEJS_BOX_PARITY.md` measures the whole surface against a Kotlin box's.

## RemoteLifecycleKotlinJs.kt { #remotelifecyclekotlinjs-kt }

The `onStart` / `onFrame` / `onStop` / `keepAlive` callbacks that every remote Kotlin/JS head shares.

[`RemoteLifecycleKotlinJs`](languages.md#remotelifecyclekotlinjs-kt-remotelifecyclekotlinjs) supplies them, with the `HeadFrame` timing record, as compiler
declarations and as a completion mirror. Callbacks register only during a Launch; a launched box
stays active until relaunch, error or Stop, and its `onStop` callbacks then run once.

## PhaseNoise.kt { #phasenoise-kt }

StackSL's phase noise family: `qnoise`, `phnoise`, `phrot` — noise whose *phase* is a control,
per frequency.

### What it is for

Two fields made from the same random kernels, differing only in phase, are related in a precise
way that no amount of offsetting or reseeding gives you. Rotate every kernel's phase by `θ`
turns and the new field correlates with the old one by `cos(2πθ)`: `0` is the same field,
`0.25` an uncorrelated partner with the same spectrum, `0.5` its negative. Rotate only the
kernels above some frequency and the two fields share their coarse structure exactly while
their fine detail decorrelates — stereo pairs, RGB channels or particle species that belong
together, and noise that churns at small scales while its large forms hold still.

Value noise (`noise`, `fbm`, `fbm3`) cannot do this. It has no phase to rotate: shifting its
output is a translation or an offset, not a phase change. These words are built from kernels
that have one — localised sinusoids, which is sparse Gabor noise.

### The construction

Each octave is a jittered lattice with one kernel per cell: a Gaussian window
`exp(-2 r²)`, truncated to zero at `r = 1.5` cells, times a sinusoid with a random direction, a
random phase, and a carrier of [`PhaseNoiseConstants.CARRIER`](languages.md#phasenoise-kt--phasenoiseconstants--carrier) cycles per cell, jittered by up to
±[`PhaseNoiseConstants.CARRIER_JITTER_OCTAVES`](languages.md#phasenoise-kt--phasenoiseconstants--carrier-jitter-octaves)/2 octaves per kernel so the spectrum is continuous
across a band rather than a comb. The same kernels are summed twice, once through `cos` and once
through `sin` — a quadrature pair — so the result is `(Nc, Ns)` and every phase rotation of it
is `Nc·cos θ − Ns·sin θ`, exactly. Each octave is divided by the square root of its own window
energy, which is independent of phase, so the identity survives normalisation.

Octave `o` is the lattice scaled by `lacunarity^o` and rotated once per octave by the fixed
([`PhaseNoiseConstants.OCTAVE_ROTATION_COS`](languages.md#phasenoise-kt--phasenoiseconstants--octave-rotation-cos), [`PhaseNoiseConstants.OCTAVE_ROTATION_SIN`](languages.md#phasenoise-kt--phasenoiseconstants--octave-rotation-sin)) pair, so a
kernel's frequency in cycles per unit of the input coordinate is its carrier times
`lacunarity^o`. That number is what a phase response sees.

### Output and range

`vec4(Nc, Ns, |N|, 1)`: the quadrature pair, its envelope (phase-invariant, so still right after
a `phrot`), and an opaque alpha. `Nc` and `Ns` are signed and zero-mean,
with an RMS near [`PhaseNoiseConstants.OUTPUT_SCALE`](languages.md#phasenoise-kt--phasenoiseconstants--output-scale)·0.7 ≈ 0.35, so they sit mostly inside
`-1..1`; `PhaseNoiseTest` pins those statistics.

### Cost

Sixteen kernels per octave, each a `sin`/`cos` pair, two hashes and an `exp`: five octaves is
eighty kernels. That is more than `fbm3` and less than `curl3`. The family is 2D over `input.xy`;
`input.w` reaches a phase response as time.

Phase is in **turns** throughout, like `phacelle`'s offset and unlike `rotate`'s radians:
`0.25` is a quarter cycle.

## StackSL.kt { #stacksl-kt }

StackSL — a concatenative shading language that compiles to GLSL, in one file with no runtime.

A StackSL program is a sequence of words over a `vec4` stack, and it lowers to exactly one GLSL
function: `vec4 stack(vec4 stack_in)`, conventionally called with `vec4(x, y, z_or_hash, time)`.
There is no interpreter here and nothing executes on the JVM — [`StackSLCompiler.compile`](languages.md#stacksl-kt--stackslcompiler--compile) is a
source-to-source translation, which is why the whole language is a compiler and a diagnostic
type and nothing else.

### The three values to know

 - [`StackSLCompileOptions`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stackslcompileoptions) decides the shape of the emitted GLSL rather than the meaning of the
   program: the symbol prefix, the entry point name, whether a header and samplers are declared,
   which textures `sample` may read, and — the one that changes semantics —
   `defaultValues`, the wrap/default convention used when a word wants an operand the stack does
   not have. `tolerant` decides whether that is a warning or an error.
 - [`StackSLCompileResult`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stackslcompileresult) is GLSL, diagnostics and an analysis. `ok` is *diagnostics with no
   ERROR*, not "the GLSL is non-empty", because a tolerant compile emits usable GLSL and
   complains at the same time.
 - [`StackSLAnalysis`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stackslanalysis) is the part worth reading before debugging a program that produced a black
   frame. Per function it reports `maxStackDepth`, `finalStackDepth`, `producedValues`,
   `usedValues` and `prunedValues`, plus [`StackSLDanglingWire`](languages.md#stacksl-kt-stacksldanglingwire) for each value that was pushed and
   never consumed. A definition whose arity does not work out is **pruned silently** in the
   emitted shader — the diagnostic and this analysis are the only places it says so.

[`compileStackSL`](languages.md#stacksl-kt--compilestacksl) and [`compileStackSLToGlsl`](languages.md#stacksl-kt--compilestacksltoglsl) are the two convenience entry points; the second
throws away everything except the source, which is usually the wrong trade.

### Where StackSL sits relative to its neighbours

`afield.stdlib/stacksl.kt` — on the [Graphics](graphics.md) page, because it is host API rather
than language — is how a box actually reaches a StackSL string. `afield.lang.rectsl` compiles through
this file: RectSL decides where rectangles are, StackSL decides how their materials shade, and
`RectSLGlsl.kt` is the join. `VolumetricNoise.kt` beside this file is the noise vocabulary the
emitted GLSL calls into.

[StackSL cheatsheet](../stacksl_cheatsheet.md) is the word-by-word reference;
[StackSL examples](../stacksl_examples.md) is the gallery.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSL.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/StackSL/)

**Used in:** [StackSL examples](../stacksl_examples.md)

## StackSLVocabulary.kt { #stackslvocabulary-kt }

The words of a small language as an editor offers them: names, stack effects and descriptions read
from the language's generated words guide, served as completions.

[`vocabularyFromGuide`](languages.md#stackslvocabulary-kt--vocabularyfromguide) reads the guide's tables, [`vocabularyCompletion`](languages.md#stackslvocabulary-kt--vocabularycompletion) offers the words at a cursor,
and [`StackSLVocabulary`](languages.md#stackslvocabulary-kt-stackslvocabulary) is StackSL's own list. `StackSLVocabularyCoverageTest` and
`LanguageVocabularyTest` cover it.

## VolumetricNoise.kt { #volumetricnoise-kt }

StackSL's volumetric noise family: `noise3`, `fbm3`, `fbmd3`, `warp3`, `curl3`, `worley3`,
`noise4`, `fbm4` — eight words that work as true 3D and 4D fields.

### Why a separate family

StackSL's original `noise` and `fbm` are two-dimensional. The word lowers to
`_noise(input.xy + input.zw * 0.07)`, so a vec4 carrying a position and a time is squashed
into a plane: z enters at one fourteenth the weight of x, as a shear rather than as a third
dimension. On a volume seen down z that reads as one fixed pattern imprinted at every depth.
The two-slice-sum workaround (`f(x,y) + f(y,z) + f(z,x)`) is what people write instead, and
it costs three fbms and does not give a 3D field — it gives three sheared 2D ones.

### Three properties the 2D words lack

**The range really is [0,1).** `_fbm(vec2)` sums five octaves at amplitudes 0.5 0.25 0.125
0.0625 0.03125, which total 0.96875, not 1 — so the usual `0.5 -` recentering leaves a
constant bias of about -0.031. A constant force integrates into a drift instead of averaging
out. Here the amplitude sum is accumulated at runtime and divided out, so the range is exactly
[0,1) for any octave count, lacunarity and gain.

**The hashes contain no `sin()`.** `_hash11(float)` uses `fract(sin(p * 127.1) * 43758.5453123)`,
and `sin` is not bit-portable: its precision is implementation-defined, it loses all meaning
for large arguments, and no CPU implementation can be trusted to agree with a GPU's.
`_hash21(vec2)` — the hash that actually feeds `_noise` and `_fbm` — has no `sin` at all; it
is `fract(p * vec2(123.34, 456.21))`, `p += dot(p, p + 45.32)`, `fract(p.x * p.y)`, so it is
already multiply/add/fract and already IEEE-754 exact. (Exact is not the same as stable:
`fract` of a large product amplifies a last-bit difference in its argument to O(1), which is
why an exactly-specified noise can still disagree visibly across backends.) The reason this
family could not use `_hash21` is dimensionality: `_hash21` takes a `vec2`, and a 3D/4D family
needs a hash over 3 and 4 inputs. The hashes below are multiply/add/fract only, which makes
[`VolumetricNoiseReference`](languages.md#volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoisereference) a real reference rather than an approximation.
`StackSLCpuVolumetricCrossCheckTest` evaluates the emitted GLSL against every function here,
bit-for-bit.

**`curl3` is divergence-free by construction.** It is the curl of a vector potential taken
with central differences at one shared epsilon. Discrete shift operators commute, so the
discrete divergence of the discrete curl cancels term for term and is zero up to float rounding
— see `VolumetricNoiseTest`. Particles advected through it swirl instead of piling into sinks.

### Constants

[`VolumetricNoiseConstants`](languages.md#volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoiseconstants) is the single source of truth for the family's shared constants —
the octave defaults, lacunarity, gain, the finite-difference epsilons, the hash multipliers and
the per-octave rotation. The Kotlin reference reads them and the emitted GLSL interpolates
them, so the two cannot drift apart. `VolumetricNoiseTest`'s `every shared constant appears in
the emitted GLSL` fails if one is ever typed into the shader text by hand. The algebraic
coefficients inside [`VolumetricNoiseReference`](languages.md#volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoisereference) — the `mix` weights, the smoothstep polynomial —
are spelled out at their call sites instead, because they are the definition of the operation
rather than a tunable value.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/VolumetricNoise.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/VolumetricNoise/)

### VolumetricNoiseReference { #volumetricnoise-kt-volumetricnoisereference }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">VolumetricNoiseReference</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/VolumetricNoise/#L177)

The CPU twin of the GLSL emitted by `volumetricNoiseHelperSource`. Every function here is a statement-for-statement transliteration of its shader counterpart, in `Float`, using only operations GLSL and the JVM both round identically. It exists so the family's semantics — ranges, continuity, `worley3`'s F1 <= F2, `curl3`'s divergence — can be asserted without a device, which is the only kind of test StackSL has ever been able to have.

## GlslAd.kt { #glslad-kt }

Reverse-mode automatic differentiation for the GLSL interpreter: `d(pixel)/d(literal)`.

`GlslAdScalars` is a `GlslScalars` instance, so a shader differentiated here runs through the
interpreter's one copy of the control flow, over the same parse tree the `Float` reference path
walks. Nothing about a GLSL builtin's *meaning* is restated; what is added is a local partial
beside each operation.

### Why reverse mode

An image loss over a wire vector is many-inputs-one-output, which is reverse mode's shape:
one forward pass plus one backward sweep answers for every wire at once, so the cost does not
grow with the number of free parameters. The loss is a **sum over pixels**, so the gradient is a
sum of per-pixel backward sweeps, one short tape per pixel, thrown away before the next. That
bounds the tape: a 64x64 fit never holds more than one pixel's operations at a time, where a
whole-image tape would hold 4096 times as many.

### The primal is bit-identical to the `Float` path

[`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) computes in `Double`, and a `Double` shader is the *wrong* shader. `GlslValue.kt`'s overview
sets out why: widening an intermediate makes the CPU result more accurate than the GPU's and
therefore a worse reference, and `fract` of a large product amplifies a last-bit difference to
O(1). On a hash-bearing program a `Double` primal would not be slightly different, it would be a
different image.

So every node this file pushes stores its value **rounded to `Float`**, at exactly the points the
`Float` path rounds. Double rounding is safe for `+ - * /` and `sqrt`: `Double` has more than
twice `Float`'s significand, so rounding a `Double`-exact sum to `Float` gives the same answer as
the `Float` operation. The differentiable pass's primal image is therefore *the same image* the
reference path produces, which `StackSLGradientTest` asserts bit for bit over a named population,
while the adjoint is the derivative of the smooth relaxation, which is the quantity a fit needs.

### Derivative conventions

 - a branch, a loop bound and an index carry **no** derivative: differentiated as taken, which
   is correct for the piecewise function away from the switch-over. `autodiff.kt` says the same.
 - `floor`, `ceil`, `trunc`, `round`, `roundEven`, `sign`, `step` and `int(...)` truncation
   carry **exactly zero** derivative. `fract` therefore carries derivative **one**, since it is
   `x - floor(x)`.
 - `abs`, `min` and `max` **split evenly at an exact tie**, which is what a central difference
   reports at a kink, so the analytic gradient and the finite-difference oracle agree there.
 - a comparison, `any`, `all`, `isnan` and `isinf` produce a derivative-free `bool`.
 - `texture()` is **refused**. A bilinear CPU texture fetch is differentiable in principle, but
   the two feedback gallery programs are already excluded from every asserted comparison in
   this backend, so a derivative through a sampler would have no oracle to check it against.
   `StackSLDifferentiabilityTest` counts it as unsupported rather than as zero.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslAd.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslAd/)

## GlslAdSurrogate.kt { #glsladsurrogate-kt }

The surrogate vocabulary a differentiable StackSL fit descends through: a mollified delta, the
jump families it may be applied to, and the schedule that narrows it.

Three types. [`AdSurrogate`](languages.md#glsladsurrogate-kt-adsurrogate) is a *temperature plus
a set of families* — the one object `GlslAdScalars` consults at each jump site.
[`AdSurrogateFamily`](languages.md#glsladsurrogate-kt-adsurrogatefamily) partitions the jump-discontinuous builtins by **where their jumps are** rather
than by name, because that is what decides the partial, and because `floor` is not one thing: as a
quantiser it is a wall worth softening, and as a noise lattice's cell index its zero is the *true*
derivative and softening it destroys a wire that already worked. [`AdAnnealing`](languages.md#glsladsurrogate-kt-adannealing) is the schedule,
and the measurements say a fit does not need it.

Nothing here is on unless a caller asks: `AdSurrogate.OFF` is the default everywhere, and even
switched on it replaces **only local partials** and never a primal value. The measurements —
including the two that argue against enabling it globally — are `dev_docs/STACKSL_SURROGATE.md`.

What is *not* here is `GlslAdScalars`' mask tracking, which is what stops a nested
predicate being charged a second kernel. That is a property of the AD path rather than of the
surrogate, so it sits in `GlslAd.kt` beside the jump sites it corrects.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslAdSurrogate.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslAdSurrogate/)

## GlslInterpreter.kt { #glslinterpreter-kt }

The evaluator for parsed GLSL shaders, tree-walking and single-threaded per invocation.

It holds no state between invocations except the globals the caller supplies, so a raster can
be rendered by running one [`GlslInvocation`](languages.md#glslinterpreter-kt-glslinvocation) per row across as many threads as there are cores
— see [`StackSLCpu`](languages.md#stackslcpu-kt-stackslcpu).

### Three design choices

**Control flow as a return value, not an exception.** Each statement reports what it did to
control flow — normal, break, continue, return or discard — as an ordinary return value, and
the caller unwinds. The tree-walking pattern normally uses a control-flow exception, but the
volumes here are large: `_fbm` returns from inside a five-iteration loop, and a 512×512 render
evaluates that `return` 1.3 million times per program, which is too many to assume a
stack-trace-bearing exception is free.

**One flat frame per function call, with block scopes as marks into it.** Entering a block
records the current top of the frame and leaving truncates back to it, giving correct GLSL
shadowing with no per-block allocation. Lookup is a backwards linear scan, which for the
emitted subset (never more than about a dozen live names) beats a hash map.

**Generic in its scalar, with exactly one copy of the control flow.** `GlslMachine` holds the
statements, the branches, the loops, the frames and the lvalue writes; what a *value* is comes
from a `GlslScalars`. `GlslScalars<GlslValue>` is the binary32 reference path and
`GlslScalars<AdValue>` makes the same shader differentiable, so `d(pixel)/d(literal)` flows
through this file rather than through a second evaluator — which would agree with itself while
both copies drifted from the spec. [`GlslInvocation`](languages.md#glslinterpreter-kt-glslinvocation) is the `Float` face of it, and is what
every pre-existing caller uses, unchanged.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslInterpreter.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslInterpreter/)

## GlslInterval.kt { #glslinterval-kt }

Interval arithmetic for the GLSL interpreter: a shader run over a whole *region* of `fragUV` at
once, returning a bound on every colour any pixel in it can produce.

`GlslIntervalScalars` is the third `GlslScalars` instance, beside the binary32 reference and the
reverse-mode one, so it runs **the emitted GLSL** through the interpreter's one copy of the
control flow. Nothing about a StackSL word is restated here.

### What is contained

The contract is the one `afield.math.functions.FnInterval` states for `Fn`, moved to binary32: for every
input inside the intervals, the value the **`Float` reference path** computes lies inside the
result (or is NaN, and the result says NaN is possible). Each operation is bounded by
[`FnRangeMath`](function.md#fninterval-kt-fnrangemath) in `Double` and the endpoints rounded *outward* to `Float`. That is sound for the
correctly rounded operations because rounding to nearest is monotone, and because a `Double`
product or sum of two floats rounds to `Float` the way the `Float` operation does (the argument
`GlslAd.kt` makes for its primal). The library transcendentals are already widened by
[`FnRangeMath`](function.md#fninterval-kt-fnrangemath), and the `Float` path rounds their `Double` result to nearest, which is monotone too.

The composite builtins (`mod`, `fract`, `mix`, `smoothstep`, `dot`, `length`) are bounded as the
`Float` path spells them, operation by operation, so the bound is of *that* arithmetic and not of
a real-number ideal. `fract(x)` gets the one structural rule `FnInterval` also has: inside one unit
cell it is endpoint-exact, across a boundary it is `[0, 1]`.

### Branches

A comparison of two overlapping intervals is neither true nor false. `truth` answers
`GlslTruth.UNKNOWN`, and `GlslMachine` then runs **both** arms from the same state and joins what
each wrote, with `join`. The machine refuses (with [`GlslUnsupported`](languages.md#glslvalue-kt-glslunsupported)) the cases a join cannot
express: arms that leave by different routes (one returns, the other falls through), and a loop
whose condition is undecided. An integer index must be a single value.

### What is refused

Builtins with no rule here are refused by name, never guessed: textures, `cross`, `reflect`,
`refract`, `faceforward`, the matrix builtins, `tan`, the inverse trigonometric and hyperbolic
functions except `tanh`, and the bit operators.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslInterval.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslInterval/)

## GlslParser.kt { #glslparser-kt }

A parser for the GLSL that StackSL's emitter actually produces.

### Why a parser and not a second backend in the compiler

`StackSLCompiler` has no symbolic node to hang a CPU arm off: its one internal node is
`StackValue(id, expression: String, …)` and `expression` is already GLSL text, built by
`String`-returning lambdas in `StackSL.kt`. Adding an `eval:` beside every `glsl:` — the
RectSL `TrackOp` shape — would mean rewriting the emitter word by word, and every one of
those rewrites is a chance to make the CPU arm disagree with the GPU arm. That disagreement
is the exact defect this backend exists to rule out: a hand-written CPU twin that diverged
from its own emitter.

Parsing the emitter's output means the CPU backend consumes *the same text the GPU consumes*,
byte for byte, and cannot drift from the shipping emitter by construction. It also needs zero
edits to `StackSL.kt`, so it cannot regress the GPU path at all.

### What the subset is, measured

Dumped for all 31 committed gallery programs (1472 lines of emitted GLSL), the entire surface
is: scalar/vector/matrix declarations, `=`/`+=`/`-=`/`*=`/`/=`, `if`, `for (int i = …; …; i++)`,
`return`, function definitions, and about 30 builtins. **No ternary, no `while`, no `switch`,
no structs, no arrays, no bit operators.** This parser covers a little more than that (ternary,
`while`, `do`, `break`/`continue`, interface blocks) so the first shader that reaches slightly
further does not fail; anything genuinely outside throws [`GlslUnsupported`](languages.md#glslvalue-kt-glslunsupported) with the token
quoted rather than guessing.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslParser.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslParser/)

## GlslScalars.kt { #glslscalars-kt }

The value type the GLSL interpreter is generic over, so that one interpreter serves both the
`Float` reference path and the differentiable one.

### One interpreter, two algebras

The interface factors out the *values*, leaving `GlslInterpreter.kt`'s machine (the statements,
the branches, the loops, the call frames, the lvalue writes) as one copy of the control flow,
shared by every scalar type. `GlslFloatScalars` is the `Float` instance, and each of its methods
is a single `GlslValue` expression, so going through the interface neither widens nor reorders
any arithmetic. `StackSLCpuFloatPathManifestTest` holds all 31 gallery programs to committed
`Float` bits.

Sharing the control flow is what lets a derivative run over **the emitted GLSL**, the artifact
the GPU consumes, rather than over a second evaluator written beside it.

`V` is a reference type in both instances ([`GlslValue`](languages.md#glslvalue-kt-glslvalue) and `AdValue`), so the `Float` path pays no
boxing for the generic parameter: one interface dispatch per operation is the entire cost.

### Why the methods take whole values

Every method here takes and returns a *whole* GLSL value rather than a component, because
`normalize`, `dot`, `length` and the matrix products are not component-wise, and an interface at
component granularity would force them to be restated per scalar. As it is, the `Float` instance
delegates to `glslMul`, `glslConstruct`, `glslSwizzle` and `GlslBuiltins.call` unchanged.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslScalars.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/GlslScalars/)

## GlslValue.kt { #glslvalue-kt }

The value model for the GLSL-subset interpreter behind StackSL's CPU backend.

### Why Float, not Double

The thing being mirrored is a GPU fragment shader whose `float` is IEEE-754 binary32. Every
intermediate here is therefore a `Float`, and every builtin rounds to `Float` at every step,
including the ones Kotlin would rather do in `Double` (`kotlin.math.sin` takes and returns
`Double`, so those are computed wide and narrowed once — see [`f1`](visualization.md#numericformatting-kt--f1)). Widening an intermediate
would make the CPU result *more* accurate than the shader and therefore a worse reference:
the goal is to reproduce the shader, not to improve on it.

Two consequences bound what any CPU implementation can agree with a GPU on, and neither is a
defect in this file:

  - `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log`, `pow`, `atan` are IMPLEMENTATION-DEFINED in GLSL. The spec
    gives them no accuracy requirement at all beyond monotonicity in places. So no CPU
    implementation can be bit-exact with a GPU's, even in principle, and any program that
    reaches one of them can only be compared under a tolerance.
  - Even the exact operations do not compose exactly, because a GPU may CONTRACT `a * b + c`
    into a fused multiply-add with one rounding while the JVM performs two. Kotlin has no
    `fma`-free guarantee to offer here either way; what it does have is no automatic
    contraction, so this interpreter is the *unfused* reading of the shader.

The interesting failure is neither of those. `fract` of a large product amplifies a last-bit
difference in its argument to O(1) — so `_hash21`, which is multiply/add/fract only and
therefore exact operation by operation, can still produce a visibly different image from a
backend that differed by one ulp three operations earlier. That is chaos, not error, and the
gallery characterisation reports it separately from tolerance.

## StackSLCpu.kt { #stackslcpu-kt }

StackSL's CPU backend: the same GLSL a GPU would run, evaluated one pixel at a time on the JVM,
so a StackSL program can be rendered, unit-tested, diffed and documented with no graphics context
at all.

[`StackSLCpu`](languages.md#stackslcpu-kt-stackslcpu) is the entry point and [`CpuRaster`](languages.md#stackslcpu-kt-cpuraster) is what comes back: RGBA floats with row 0 at the
top, quantised the way a `VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM` attachment does, and encodable straight to
PNG. `StackSLCpu.renderStill` is the one-liner a box wants.

What the backend is exact about is the *program*. `StackSLCpu.renderFragment` takes a complete
fragment shader as text and knows nothing about StackSL; the StackSL half compiles a program with
`StackSLCompiler` and substitutes the result into a `{{ stack.auto.<slot> }}` template, which is
the same tag the production expansion path in `afield.graphics.shader.shaders` fills. Both paths therefore
receive the same string, and nothing about a word's behaviour is restated here: change what the
emitter makes of `fbm` and this backend changes with it on the next call, with no edit. Tests pin
the two copies that make that true: `StackSLCpuExpansionTest` compares the compile options against
the production path's, and `StackSLCpuStillTemplateTest` compares the gallery's fragment template
against the committed one in the gallery workspace.

It is a reference, not a renderer. It is an interpreter, so it is orders of magnitude short of a
GPU, and `StackSLCpu.renderStill` states a cost for one program at one size. It is not bit-exact
either: GLSL leaves `sin`, `cos`, `exp`, `log`, `pow` and `atan` implementation-defined, so a
program that reaches one of them can only be compared under a tolerance. [`GlslValue`](languages.md#glslvalue-kt-glslvalue) has that
argument in full, including the case where operations that *are* exact still diverge visibly.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/StackSLCpu.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/StackSLCpu/)

## StackSLCpuGallery.kt { #stackslcpugallery-kt }

Compares StackSL's CPU renderer against the GPU: 31 committed gallery programs, each with its
fragment template and the 512x512 PNG a real GPU drew for it.

`public/docs/assets/stacksl_gallery/` holds, per gallery entry `<name>`, the program
(`<name>_stackSL_.stacksl`), its fragment shader with the literal `{{ stack.auto.program }}` slot
(`<name>_fragment_.glsl`), and its `docOrder` / `animate` / `timeSpeed` / `feedback` settings
(`<name>_metadata_.yaml`). `public/docs/assets/stacksl/stacksl-<name>.png` is the GPU's still.

The fragment file is a template, not expanded GLSL, so a CPU render that reads it goes through the
live `StackSLCompiler`, and both backends are compared against today's emitter. 29 of the 31
templates are byte-identical (`fragmentTemplate(1.75f)` in `StackSLGalleryHarness`); the other 2
are the feedback template.

The ground truth is 8-bit. The harness renders into `VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_SRGB` and clamps to
`[0,1]` first, so the GPU's answer is known to one sRGB level. Agreement is therefore measured in
8-bit sRGB levels, with the CPU side encoded the same way ([`StackSLCpuGallery.galleryArgb`](languages.md#stackslcpugallery-kt--stackslcpugallery--galleryargb)), and
"exact" means "quantises to the same byte".

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/StackSLCpuGallery.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/StackSLCpuGallery/)

### AgreementTier { #stackslcpugallery-kt-agreementtier }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">AgreementTier</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">label</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">why</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/cpu/StackSLCpuGallery/#L77)

Why a program is or is not entitled to agree tightly, decided from the **emitted GLSL text** rather than from a hand-kept list, so a program that gains an `fbm` gets reclassified without anyone remembering to.

Constants: `EXACT_OPS`, `SMOOTH_TRANSCENDENTAL`, `HASH21_AMPLIFIED`, `HASH11_UNBOUNDED`, `FEEDBACK`.

## StackSLFit.kt { #stackslfit-kt }

Gradient descent on a StackSL program's own literals: fit a shader to a picture, then write the
fitted numbers back into the program.

### Why a StackSL program is differentiable

StackSL is not geometry. It is a **per-pixel field**: `main()` runs once per pixel with `fragUV`
as its only spatial input, and the output is an ordinary composition of arithmetic and GLSL
builtins. So `d(pixel)/d(wire)` is the chain rule. There is no rasteriser in the pipeline, no
coverage term, no approximation and so no bias to characterise.

RectSL, a shape language, is the harder case. There a pixel's value depends on a parameter
through *coverage*, so `d(pixel)/d(parameter)` needs a differentiable rasteriser, and a coverage
approximation is a modelling choice with a bias to characterise. `RectSLSoftRaster.kt` is that
choice, made there.

### Limits on what a fit can do

 1. **A fit can only move literal-backed wires.** See [`StackSLWires`](languages.md#stackslwires-kt-stackslwires): a wire noted
    `"optional default palette a"` is a default the emitter supplied, with no literal in the
    source to rewrite. [`StackSLFitResult.fittedIndices`](languages.md#stackslfit-kt--stackslfitresult--fittedindices) is the population that moved and
    [`WiredProgram.wires`](languages.md#stackslwires-kt--wiredprogram--wires) is the larger set that exists.
 2. **The template clamps.** `StackSLCpu.stillTemplate`, the default, ends `main()` with
    `outColor = vec4(clamp(c, 0.0, 1.0), 1.0)`, and `clamp` carries zero derivative outside its
    range. A pixel that is saturated at the seed therefore contributes **nothing** to the
    gradient, so a seed whose image is mostly blown out is a seed with almost no signal.
    [`StackSLFitResult.saturatedFraction`](languages.md#stackslfit-kt--stackslfitresult--saturatedfraction) measures how much of the image is in that state.
 3. **The default loss is a per-pixel sum of squares and rewards exactly that.** It has no term
    for structure, so a fit can lower it a long way by matching a target's colour and luminance
    statistics while the image does not resemble the target at all. `StackSLFitFigureTest`
    writes a figure of the target, the seed and the fit side by side, which is the comparison
    the loss itself cannot make. `StackSLFitLoss.LPIPS` descends on the perceptual distance
    instead, with the gradient of the LPIPS network chained through the program
    ([`StackSLLpipsLoss`](languages.md#stacksllpipsloss-kt-stacksllpipsloss)); `StackSLFitLoss.LPIPS_PIXEL` on the mean of the two.

## StackSLIntervals.kt { #stackslintervals-kt }

Interval bounds on a fragment shader's colours: a certified range for every pixel in a rectangle,
without rendering the pixels.

[`StackSLIntervals`](languages.md#stackslintervals-kt-stackslintervals) encloses a rectangle ([`StackSLRegionBound`](languages.md#stackslintervals-kt-stackslregionbound)) or splits the frame into a quadtree
of tiles ([`StackSLTile`](languages.md#stackslintervals-kt-stacksltile)) proven flat to a tolerance; [`StackSLTilePicture`](languages.md#stackslintervals-kt-stacksltilepicture) draws the result.

## StackSLWires.kt { #stackslwires-kt }

StackSL's dangling wires, made runnable on the CPU: the free-parameter vector a fit descends.

`StackSLCompileOptions.externalizeConstants` already lifts every numeric literal out of a
program into an emitted `float` array called `<prefix>_wires`, with a `<prefix>_init_wires`
initialiser, and records each one as a `StackSLDanglingWire` carrying its `index`, its
`initial`, and the source `token` it came from. So the parameter vector needs no new syntax.

### Why the emitted GLSL has to be rewritten first

This backend **cannot parse the externalised GLSL at all**. `GlslParser` refuses arrays outright
(`"GLSL arrays are not in the StackSL subset"`, on both the global and the local declaration
path) and `StackSLCpu.stackAutoOptions` pins `externalizeConstants = false`. Two further things
break even if arrays are granted: every emitted function gains a trailing
`, float <prefix>_wires[<prefix>_wire_count]` parameter, and the entrypoint gains a **second,
overloaded** one-argument wrapper that declares the array, calls the initialiser and forwards.
`GlslShader.functions` is keyed by name, so the wrapper simply replaces the real function.

[`lower`](languages.md#stackslwires-kt--stackslwires--lower) closes that with one source-to-source rewrite of the **emitted** GLSL, so what the CPU
runs is still the artifact the GPU consumes rather than a restatement of it:

 1. element *i* of `<prefix>_wires` becomes a scalar global `<prefix>_wire_i`, a shape the
    subset does support, and one a caller can push a new value into per evaluation with
    `setGlobal`, with no recompile;
 2. the wire parameter and the wire argument disappear from every signature and call;
 3. `const int <prefix>_wire_count`, `<prefix>_init_wires` and the forwarding wrapper are
    dropped, the initial values having moved into the globals.

`StackSLWireLoweringTest` renders the lowered program with every wire at its recorded initial
and asserts the raster is **bit-identical** to the ordinary non-externalised compile of the
same program.

### Which wires can be written back

A wire's `note` says where it came from, and that is what governs the round trip. A `"number"`
wire stands for a literal the human typed, so a fitted value can be substituted at the recorded
`line`/`column` and the program still reads as the program. A wire noted
`"optional default palette a"` is a default the *emitter* supplied for a word that was given no
operand: there is no literal in the source to rewrite, and inventing one would mean pushing four
`vec4`s in front of `palette`. So [`rewrite`](languages.md#stackslwires-kt--stackslwires--rewrite) fits and rewrites **literal-backed wires only**,
[`literalBacked`](languages.md#stackslwires-kt--stackslwires--literalbacked) is the population, and the rest are held at their initials. A program's wire
count is therefore an upper bound on its fittable parameter count rather than the count itself,
and [`StackSLFit`](languages.md#stackslfit-kt-stackslfit) reports both.

## EmbeddedStackSL.kt { #embeddedstacksl-kt }

vocabulary, and each line's stage as a line note.

[`EmbeddedStackSL`](languages.md#embeddedstacksl-kt-embeddedstacksl) finds those strings by a leading `#stacksl` line or by assignment to one of the
box's `stack.auto` slots, as the text is typed.

## StackAutoCard.kt { #stackautocard-kt }

Sliders under a box for the numbers in its `stack.auto` slots, redrawing the box's own shader
without a recompile.

[`StackAutoCard`](languages.md#stackautocard-kt-stackautocard) writes each slider to the slot's uniform block, can keep the numbers back into the
box's `code`, and shows the slot either in its host shader or alone on the study frame.
[`installStackAutoCard`](languages.md#stackautocard-kt--installstackautocard) registers it.

## StackAutoStudy.kt { #stackautostudy-kt }

Studies of the `stack.auto` slots in a box's own shaders: checked edits to a slot's StackSL, and
pictures of it in its host shader and alone.

[`StackAutoStudies`](languages.md#stackautostudy-kt-stackautostudies) finds or makes the [`StackAutoSlotStudy`](languages.md#stackautostudy-kt-stackautoslotstudy) for a slot, and [`StackAutoView`](languages.md#stackautostudy-kt-stackautoview) draws the
two pictures: where the slot's module is drawn, and the slot's program by itself on the study frame.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackAutoStudy.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackAutoStudy/)

## StackAutoStudyTools.kt { #stackautostudytools-kt }

The tools an AI4 conversation gets when it is opened on the code of a box whose shaders have
`{{ stack.auto.<slot> }}` slots with programs bound.

Each works on one slot's study (see [`StackAutoStudies`](languages.md#stackautostudy-kt-stackautostudies)), inside the box's own shader: the end
result is what the tools show.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackAutoStudyTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackAutoStudyTools/)

**Used in:** [Talking to the StackSL in your shader](../stackauto_conversation.md), [StackSL examples](../stacksl_examples.md)

## StackSLGpu.kt { #stackslgpu-kt }

Where a StackSL study's frames come from: the GPU when a window is running, the CPU reference
otherwise.

Both sides implement [`StackSLRasterizer`](languages.md#stackslgpu-kt-stackslrasterizer) and hand back raw-output rasters with rows top to bottom
and `uv.y` upwards, so every measurement a study makes is independent of the renderer:
[`StackSLGpuRasterizer`](languages.md#stackslgpu-kt-stackslgpurasterizer) and [`CpuStackSLRasterizer`](languages.md#stackslgpu-kt-cpustackslrasterizer).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLGpu.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLGpu/)

## StackSLPrograms.kt { #stackslprograms-kt }

StackSL as a main language for a box's children: compile on run, draw in the window above, and check
each run in as a study revision.

[`StackSLPrograms`](languages.md#stackslprograms-kt-stackslprograms) is the entry point; [`StackSLLive`](languages.md#stackslprograms-kt-stacksllive) follows a running program's edits in its window,
and [`StackSLExecution`](languages.md#stackslprograms-kt-stackslexecution) is the box execution that runs it. [`installStackSLLanguage`](languages.md#stackslprograms-kt--installstacksllanguage) registers the
language.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLPrograms.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLPrograms/)

## StackSLStudy.kt { #stackslstudy-kt }

The revisioned study behind every StackSL program: checked edits, history on disk, and the
measurements a model and a person work from.

[`StackSLStudy`](languages.md#stackslstudy-kt-stackslstudy) holds one program's revisions and renders them through the CPU reference, so
observing, tracing, sweeping a knob and comparing two revisions give the same pixels in a test, a
headless run and a live session.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudy.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudy/)

## StackSLStudyShader.kt { #stackslstudyshader-kt }

The single fragment shader a StackSL study renders through, with its CPU, WebGL2 and knob-finding
uses.

[`StackSLStudyShader`](languages.md#stackslstudyshader-kt-stackslstudyshader) fixes the study frame, `program(vec4(uv, hash, seconds))` on a unit square with
`y` upwards, and finds the numbers a person typed so they can be turned and written back.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyShader.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyShader/)

### StackSLStudyShader { #stackslstudyshader-kt-stackslstudyshader }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">StackSLStudyShader</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyShader/#L48)

The one shader a StackSL study renders through, and the three things done with it: render on the CPU (the evidence a model is shown), translate to WebGL2 (the live preview a person turns knobs on), and find the numbers a person typed (the knobs).

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="stackslstudyshader-kt--stackslstudyshader--reference-time"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">const</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">REFERENCE&#95;TIME</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyShader/#L51) | The time a single still is rendered at, matching the StackSL gallery's stills. |
| <a id="stackslstudyshader-kt--stackslstudyshader--fragment"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">FRAGMENT</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyShader/#L57) | The study's fragment shader: the StackSL gallery's animated template. ## StackSLStudyTools.kt { #stackslstudytools-kt }

The tools an AI4 conversation gets when it is opened on a StackSL program's `stackSL` property.

Each works on the focused box's own study (see [`StackSLPrograms`](languages.md#stackslprograms-kt-stackslprograms)), so nothing here is per
document. A document can still add tools of its own from a box: [`AgentToolExtensions.register`](machine-learning.md#agenttoolextensions-kt--agenttoolextensions--register)
with its document as the scope.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyTools.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyTools/)

**Used in:** [Talking a shader into existence](../stacksl_conversation.md)

## StackSLStudyViewer.kt { #stackslstudyviewer-kt }

The output card a person uses on a StackSL study: a live WebGL2 preview, sliders for the typed
numbers, per-line stages, variants and history.

[`StackSLStudyViewer`](languages.md#stackslstudyviewer-kt-stackslstudyviewer) makes the same transactions on the study as the model's tools, so a knob kept
on the card becomes a checked revision like any other edit.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyViewer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/stacksl/study/StackSLStudyViewer/)
